Tea el ld Sir Andrew Clarke, For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital : "Tea lea blessed beverage. I donot know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock. when I get into a place, the lad, of the hone(' will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say ' thank you very much_ But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills the cup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of all Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful in its effects upon the nervous system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Slack China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspoonful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within live minutes you must pour It off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for goblin what this old fashioned teals like. The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the system, and if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. This old fashioned China Tea, as recommended by Sir Andrew Clarke, can be obtained now, as always or the last 35 years, at

TEE fellow whose head wasturned was a wooden- head, of course. THE more a woman's waist is shaped like an hour-glass, the sooner will her sands of We run out. Warr is that which is always invisible yet never out of sight? The letter "I," which is always in visible. CERTAINLY you understand that the opponenL. of the further coinage of silver are not buy -metallists. Tnene was a great military ball at Aldershot last week. In fact, it is still there—a cannon shot weighing LOSI pounds. IT is generally supposed that when a fellow wins the love of a girl he has her confidence. Per contra, it is a case of downright Miss trust. Two farmers had a dispute about the boundary lines of their farms. Their dispute is now settled, and so are the lawyers—on their farms. Tat Hartford Post says "it looks very much as if the days of the Mormons were drawing to a close." Guess that is so as of ten as once in twenty- four hours. A vistree. in Dublin was asked by a car-driver if he wanted a car. " No' " said he; "I ate able to walk." "May your honour long be able but seldom willing," was the witty rejoinder. AN Irishman, speaking of a friend who he suspected of living altogether beyond his means, .observed that he believed he would owe several thousand pounds after all his debts were paid. A NEW evening paper tells us that " sailors are never so much at sea as when they are on shore." In this they are somewhat like hen- pecked husbands, who are never so much at heme as when they are abroad. aeli I hear u man cry out " It's a bad world I" I must, of coarse, lump him with the aggregate Iniquity; for how can he have the enormous vanity to select himself as the one pure Adam from the naughty millions ?"—Dseagles Jerrold. AN optimist is a weman with -a new 'summer bonnet. A pessimist is a woman without a new summer bonnet. An optimist is a man with a baby one day old. A pessimist is a man with a baby one hundred and eighty-three nights -old, and 'teething. CHARLET IL being in company with Lord Rochester and others of the nobility, Killigrew -came in. 4' Now," says the King, "we shall hear of our faults." "No, faith," Killigrew, "I don't -care to trouble my head with that 'which all the town talks of." LILY (secretary of the cooking class)—" Now, girls, we've learned nine cakes, two kinds of angel food, and seven pies. What next?" Susie (engaged)—" Dick's father says I must learn to make bread." Indignant Chorus--"Rread ? Absurd! What.are bakers for'?" SOME of the old Roman gladiators were armed with a trident and a net. A net is a very effeative weapon now. A hornet will scatter a picnic party, .aad,a cornet will break up 4 • quiet neighbourhood. 64.1 TELL you," said Poots, " there's an indescrib- able sense of luxury in lying 'in bed and ringing 'ones bell for one's valet." "You got a 'valet !" • exolaimed Pcots's friend. "No," replied Poets; 44. but I've got a bell !" A •GENTLICAAII observed -to 'Dr. Johnson ' that there were fewer vagrant poor in Scotland than in ;Legland, and as a proof of it said there was no instance of a beggar dying in the streets there. "I believe you are very right, sir," says Johnson, but that does not arise from want cif vagrante, Ibut the impossibility of starving a Scotchman." "BY heavens! that stuff is not fit-for a hog to eat!" remarked Smythe, as be pushed away his plate of beef stew at the Jarby boarding-house, the other day, at dinner. " Allright ; you needn't. eat It then, sir," spoke up Mrs. Jarby. " WHAT do those letters stand fee?" asked a •ourious wife to her husband, as he 'looked at his masonic seal. "Well, really, my love," he replied •enoonragiegly, "I presume it is because they can" sit down." the postponed further questioning. A LEGAL CONUNDRUM.—" Judge," said a lawyer to an old jurist, "if a man is in doubt as to whether he shall kiss a pretty girl or not, what should he do ?" " Give toe pretty girl the benefit .of the doubt, by all means," emphatically answeted

the judge. How AN AGENT COT OVER A DLEFICtTLTY. —A -young man living in Leadville forwarded to his little brother in St. Louis, as a present, a choice donkey of the diminutive species known as the Mexican burro. The transportation agent, in making out his list, concluded that' burro" meant "bureau," and so reported to his ouperior" one bureau missing, and one jackass over." ME.. A. CHERRY, an actor, was written to with an offer for a very capital engagement from a man. ager who on a former occasion had not behaved altogether well to him. Cherry sent him word that he had been bitten by him, and he was resolv- ,ed that he should not make "two bites -of A. Cherry." " THERE is A use for cats," says the Torolgo Globe, " and a necessity for dogs; circumstances justify babies and throw a halo of extenuation about the milkman and the ,fishmonger, the ',claw grinder' and the mender of old umbrellas; but he that keepeth a peacock or a shrieking parrot within city limita is utterly without excuse." DAVID DALE, who was a man of short stature, on entering his counting-house one frosty mon complained of the state of the streets, mentioned that he had "fallen a' his length?" "And what of that, air?" remarked an old book- keeper, "I'm sure a gentleman o' your height .couldna fa' ony great length." HELPING HIS MASTED.—A gentleman was at dinner, and a servant boy, lately engaged, was handing him a tray of liquors in different sized .glasses. Being in the middle of an anecdote to his neighbour, he mechanically held out his hand to- wards the tray; but, as people often do when they are thinking of something else, he did not take a glass. The boy thought he was hesitating which liquor he would have, and, like a good fellow, wishing to help his master, he pointed to one par- ticular glass, and whispered "That's the biggest,

sir." - DiemNo the temporary separation of Lord Avon. more and Curran, Egan espoused the Judge's imaginary quarrel so bitterly that a duel was the consequence. The parties met, and on the ground Egan complained that the disparity in their sizes gave his antagonist a manifest advantage. "I might as well fire at a razor's edge as at him," said Egan. "and he may hit me as easily as a turf stack." "I'll tell you what, Mr. Egan," replied Curran; "I wish to take no advantage of you— let my size be chalked out upon your side, and I am quite content that every shot which hits outside that mark should go for nothing," A Jeavisu gentleman went into a restaurant to get his dinner, and the devil of temptation whispered into his ear. "Eat some bacon." He knew that if there was anything in the universe calculated to excite the wrath of the Infinite Being, Who made every shining star, it was to see a gentleman eating bacon. He knew it, and he knew the Infinite Being was looking. But his appetite got the better of his conscience—as it Gaon has with as all—and he ate the bacon. Ile knew it was wrong. When he went into that restaurant the weather was delightful, the sky was 118 blue as Tune, and when he came out the sky was covered with angry clouds, the lightning leaping from one to the other, and the earth shaking beneath the voice of the thunder. He went back into that restaurant with a face as white as milk, and he said to one of the waiters, "My goodness! did you ever hear such a fuss about a little piece of bacon?" The great Italian composer apparently anticipates the tame when a man, with no selection from the alphabet after his name, will be as distinguished as was the undeco- rated Englishman amid the beribboned members of the Berlin Labor Congress.

By order of the Czar, the officers of a certain regi- ment of Horse Guards, stationed at Charkoff, are to pay the widow of a merchant murdered in that city a yearly pension of 5,000 roubles. The deceased merchant met his death at the hands of men belong- ing to the •regiment, and the Czar has made the officers responsible, saying that they were to blame for the loose discipline which made such a crime possible.

The death of Prince Victor of llohenlohe has >up- set all the Court arrangements, and also the in- tended hospitalities of the Prinoo and Princess of Wales at Sandringham, where there is not now likely` to be either a ball or a lawn meet .of the hounds this winter. The contemplated tableaux and theatrienls at Osborne, and other projected enter- tainments, have been abandoned, and the ,Queen has given up her intention of,opening Parliament, and will now remain quietly in the Isle el Wight untilwithin a few days of the Royal wedding.

A -correspondent writes " Star" an who ferreted out the Benjamin letter in the Great Spink Pearl case is badly wanted in Melbourne just now. Madame Melba, the respondent in a princely divorce case in the early future,' has written to tiler father in'•llelbourne, Mr. David Mitchell, a letter, of need- less to say, highly interesting character. It is locally understood to have been on the strength of this letter that the family solicitors took the un- us-aal course of writing to the Melbourne papers protesting Madame Melba's absolute innocence of the charges alleged against her. The Melbourne pressmen are striving all they know to get a glimpse di Madame Melba's letter, but so far ovithout suc- oess.

M. Emile de Laveieye, the great Belgian econom- ist, whose death haejust occurred so ,nnexpectedly, bad many titles tokfame. Among other things he was the first to propose a municipal•death duty on 1 houses and land as a form of taxation eminently suited to oblige the owners of the ground values of London to contribute to the expenses of the govern- ment of the town. M. de Laveleye gave as his reason for the proposal that ib wssalorm of taxation which it was practically imnossiblefor the landlord to pass on to his tenant. "Peoplesseldom speculate in their own death" was the phrase he used when he first proposed the scheme to a small band of English friends 'who were staying with him in a beautiful retreat overlooking the Lake of Geneva.

In Miss" Margo" Tennant, whom Lord Rosebery is to marry shonly, the lord of Dalmeny will take to wife one of the finest horsewomen in England. Miss Tennant is•not only a good rider—perfect in all the technical excellences of the saddle—but she is also a regnlar devil-may-care cross-cogntry dasher. Last year she stayed for some time with the Earl and Countess Spencer at Altborpe, North- amptonshire, and hunted with tho Pytchley hounds of which Lord Spencer is master. She had her own hunters with her, and her hard•fding across some of the splendid hunting-country, which Major Whyte-Melville has described in his novels, was quite sensational ; and hard riding is pretty well known in the Pytchley country. During the famous baccarat trial last year it may be remem- bered that Miss Tennant was one of the most noticed women in court; indeed she could hardly fail to attract notice wherever she went.

There is talk of yet another" satiety "trial which will cause some stir, though happily it will be free from repulsive,details of the kind that have dis- gusted all decently minded people with the causes Mara of 1894. The action will, it is said, be one for slander, and,will be brought by one Well-known London hostess against another both the ladies, it appeats,independently fixed upon the same evening for a dance,and invited very much the Caine set. It was not till some days after the invitations were is- sued that the discovery was made that the fixtures clashed. Both entertainers were, of course,at their wit's end to know how to outwit their rivals. One of the ladies, however, bethoughttherself of the de- vice of wiring round to the most desirable guests that there was scarlet fever at the other house, and as a consequence her party wash success and her rival's a failure. The legality of this social strata- gem is to be decided in court.

Sir William Thomson is the first peer who owes his title to scientific eminence, for this was hardly the case with Lord Armstrong. The new peer can afford it. Apart 'from his professional income his patents bring him in about .£8,060 a year. It was he who conceived the electromotors4 which indicate and self-register the most subtle electric changes in the atmosphere. He has converted water at the freezing point into ice without the expenditure of force, and is the inventor of wonderful and delicate instruments for the preservation of cables under water. Scotchmesa lose sight of his political crank- iness in view of his splendid scientific achievement, and no name is more revered by Glasgow students. Sir William Thomson has ever stoutly opposed the extreme Sabbatarienism of Scotland. He would open museums and libraries on Sundays, and has taken an active part in the Sunday lecture more- -1 nasntin Glasgow, to the disgust and horror of the uncoguid."

American schoolboys appear to be very much like English schoolboys, at least in their fancy for inscribing their school books with rhymed warnings against the practice of book pilfering. -•` Steal not this bothk for fear of shame," with its solemn admonitions regarding pains and penalties'here and hereafter is probably not unknown among them, since a gentleman at Lancaster, Pennsylvania, has found in a well-thumbed grammar the following stanza, which is familiar ,enough in some of our old grammar schools: My book is a thing, My fist is another : If you steal the one, You will feel the other. Another rhyme, found by the same gentleman, in the book of a Pennsylvanian schoolboy, has, 'how- ever, a decidedly trans-Atlantic flavour: If this book gets off the track, _ .
Give it a kick and send it back To Robert Brown,
ANOTHER GUN FATUITY.

Two young men, named Ross and McLean, were shooting near Ruthven, Forfarshire, on Tuesday, when one of the guns exploded, killing McLean on the spot, and terribly shattering the lower part of Ross's face. Ross managed to walk to a house near which the acci- dent occurred, but was unable to give an intelligible statement of the circumstances.

div.head: GENERAL BOOTH'S INDIAN TOUR.
div.p: GENERAL BOOTH'S INDIAN TOUR.

SCENE AT AHMEDABAD. General Booth has just concluded a very successful campaign in Guzerat. I number of crowded high-caste meetings have been held, at which much enthusiasm was displayed. At Ahmedabad, on Sunday evening there was a great display. The grounds in which the gather— ing was held were lit by 5,000 lamps. Ten thousand Hindoos, 150 officers, 2,500 soldiers, and some men of Camel Corps of the Bheel contingeht were present. One hundred and twenty Hindoos professed salvation, General Booth, who is in good health, is proceeding to Calcutta.

yes, I ant again sailing. Again in the steerage, and again sick at the stomach, and sick at heart. I have long hoped to be at rest •; this hope deferred, is making the heart grow sick. California is now a long way behind me, and so also are those I love so dearly; and what is worse, I have no idea when I shall see them again. Well, cheer up ; a long Jane that has no turning. When it was decided I ,should leave` Frisco," it was also decided I should get to New York, BY WAY or PANAMA. To go ovecland would have cost near 70 dollars, To go by sea, the fare is 40 dollars. The former takes a week, the latter near five weeks. I am, in a sense, not sorry I chose the latter; a great deal is to be seen. Still, if I had fully comprehended the menotony of the journey—l ;had not forgotten the steerage of the Egypt—l should have hesitated a little longer ere undertaking the voyage. On the 13th -of November, I secured my bunk in the City of New York, sailing the same day, after quite a deluge of weepinge and wonderings as to when we-should all meet again. I was soon outside the Gcaden Gates of 'Frisco,a city whose streets are not paved with gold, and whosecitizens are in complete ignorance as to the first principles of common hon- esty. ‘• Husslers and Russiers " are the characters 'wanted; men of selfish nature, whose God is the Almighty dollar. I don't say this out of any ill-feel- ing fer the place. The daily press of the city fully proves what I say. Now-for our ship; my home for the next month, or more. When we had pulled ourselves together, and looked around a little, we tound ourselves a motley crew. Some of your read- ers will be able to fancy for themselves what the size of the steerage -may be in a troop ship of 1,900 tons burthen. Out of this has to be taken the fore- castle in which the sailors find sleeping room ; the rest belongs to-us—the steerage passengers.. Fifty white menonchiding 12 "old salts" returning from the Behriag-sea; a hundred Chinamen, and a few Mexicans. +Quite a picked lot. Whatpleasure should have had, had it been rough weather! Since we left the-city, never a ripple has disturbed the ivater. For two weeks—' "The skylairbeen bright, with sunshine above ,us, And the sea-asleep at our feet."

Not for =any hour; have we at any time been , eut- side of land,.yet the first few days were monotonous. During the day nothing to do bat sit on deck'read- ing or playing draughts. We managed to have the " pigtails" sloeping quarters made off separate with sail-cloth. They are not bad fellows when let alone, but therare an awful nuisance with their music. While 1. am-writing, their band is in full go, with a drum -something like a tambourine, and a lot of string 'instruments of the most -singular shapes. Therean, along with their screeching voices, man- age to make a noise more like a bedlam than any- thingelse I can fancy. The " Man o' War's " men are •a fine lot of fellows, full of yarns which we all like to,lieten to. To see us all on the top deck rolling.ahout under the awning would4ust amuse some of you landlubbers. Four days' sailing brought us to •

In a sermon just published on "gratitude for 1 deliverance from thb grave," the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon deals with the subject of presentiments in the following characteristic way : Ido not think that I am superstitious: I fancy that I am pretty clear of that vice ; yet I have had presentiments concerning things to oome or not to I come; and, moreover, I have met with so many 1 Christian men who, in the time of trouble, have received singular warnings, or sweet assurances of coming deliverance, that I am bound to believe that the Lori does sometimes whisper to the heart of his children, and assure them in trial that they shall not be crushed, and in sickness that they shall not die. Haw do you understand the story of John Wycliffe, at Lutterworth, in any other way than this? He had been speaking against the monks, and various abuses of thechurch. He was the first man known to history that preached the gospel in Eng- land during the Popish ages—we know him as the Morning Star of the Reformation. He was a man so great that, if he had possessed a printing-press, we might never heve needed a Luther; for he had even clearer light than that great Reformer. He lacked the means.of spreading his doctrine, which the heart of printing supplied. He did much: he prepared everything to Luther's hand; and Luther was but the prochtimer of Wyclife's doctrine. Wycliffe was ill—very ill, and the friars came round him, like crows round a dying sheep, They pro- fessed to be full of tender pity; but they were right glad that their enemy was going to die. So they said to him, .• Do you not repent? Before we can give you the viaticum—the last oiling before you die—would it not be well to retract the hard things which you have said against the zealous Friars, and ibis Holiness of Rome? We are eager to forget the past, and give you the last Sacrament in peace." Wycliffe begged an attendant to help ,li fill to sit up ; and 'then he cried with all his strength, "I shall not die, but live, to declare the works of the, Lord, and to expose the wickedness of the Friars.", He did 'not die, either: death himself could not have killed him then; for he had mart work to do,: and the Lord made him immortal till it was done. How could Wycliffe know that he spoke truly ? Certainly he was free from all foolhardy brag ; hal there was upon his mind a foreshadowing of future work that he had to do, and he felt that he couM not die till it was accomplished. Now, do not be making up presentiments about all -sorts of things. , because I have said that sometimes Mile Lord grants them to his Saints. This would be a mischievous piece of absurdity. I remember a young woman who lived not far from here, who had a presenti- ment that she would die. I do notthink that there . _

_ was really much the matter with her; but she re- fused to eat, and was likely to be,etarved. I went to see her, and she told me that She had a presenti- ment that she should die, and therefore she should not waste food by eating it. She spoke to me very I-solemnly about this presentimentomd I replied" I ••believe there may be such things." Yes: she was • sure I was on her side! Then I \went on to say, I once had a presentiment that I was a donkey,and it turned out true in my case:;,aud now I had much the same presentiment about-her. This surprised her, and I asked her friends to bring her food. She said she would not sat it; and then I told her that if she was resolved on suicide. I would mention it at a church meeting that evening, and put her out of church, since we could not have suicides in our membership. She could not bear to be.put out of the church, and began to eat,and it turned out that: my presentiment about her was correct:; she had. been foolish, and she had the good sense to see that it was so. I felt bound totell you this story, lest }on should fancy that I would support 'you in sen- timental nonsense. While there are so many stupid people in the world, we have need to give cautions where the wise do not need them.

div.head: ILkZATL.EN IN M=CO,
div.p: ILkZATL.EN IN M=CO,

where'vre stayed a day and a half. Of,course we must go on shore. For this a charge of dol. is tuade.by the boatman. I fear Icannot describe this Mexican town. It was certainly a mostinteresting sight. Long rows of low adobe houses, the cocoa nut,.the banana, and the orange trees lining the streets and forming shady walks, shied us from analmost vertical sun. The men and women all of arid' copper colour, and clothed in the garb of 'chastity. I must suppose this, as there was little clothing to be seen. After staying here a day and a half, we sailed for San Bias. Thisple.ce differed very little from the previous .one, only that it was hotter. Oh, the heat was now getting fearful, and when some of us passengers got on shore, we differed very little from the natives -se far as dress was concerned. Now fruit began ,to,be plentiful, butwe were warned not toeat much,as all sorts of malarial ailments were likely to follow the eating. A.few of us set off for a walk in the woods. 'Think of it, walking under the cocoa nut . and banana trees, and keeping watch lest we tread on a ser- pent or run our shins against the prickly cactus. I should like to have brought away a few specimens of-the prickly plants whilst a-broad. Alline country for sun and fruit, but an awful country for insects and reptiles. We went into a dine church here which seemed to be under repair. I say" seemed " because there were some workmen about, but they don't tike life here as they do in 'Frisco. Everybody seems to think that swinging in a hammock isdust exer- tion enough. The church was, of course, Roman Catholic. One should go through these 'Mexican towns to see the Roman Catholic religion at its best, ormorst. The Most stupid ignoralice,.coupled with thievishness goes along well with thetChurch of Rome: Memwith the likeness of some -favourite saint hanging down between their shoulders, will -ease our pockets if they have the least chance, but then we were only heretics. I went to •say, if I can getit down, that this church was set with brick from Staffordshire. Donkeys about here.; they and mules seem to do all the work. I saw tons of iron doubled into shape to fit the poor mule's back. A sad state of morals rules here: mothers, daughters, indeed the whole family, male and fermale,aeem not to know what virtue is. I managed to introduce myself to the master of one house, a Greek, who had married (?) a Mexican woman.

BAKING WAS GOING ON. The dough was on the flat side of a large stone. With a flat piece of wood dough, the size of an orange, was taken up, and by patting with the palms of the hands, was soon beaten ant to the size of a pancake, then it was placed in a pan on a few embers, and was soon baked. Their houses .and fire- places are about as primitive as can well be imag- ined. ' Very little attempt is made at privacy, nor yet at protection against robbery. I suppose they only think heretics fair game for their thievish- ness. Leaving San Blas, we made for Mangonollo, of which place pretty well the same description bolds good. The loading and unloading of the ship at these places is hard work for the natives, hat:finds i them aciew dollars. At none of these places can the ship unload, except through lighters: These in their turn have to be unloaded by inen wading in up to their necks and tremendous burdens these men do carry. After a. day's stay here we started for Ampule°, Nib* we' stayed two weary days. A big rambling Place this, if possible more primitive than the others. Fruit was cheaper, oranges and pine apples were plentiful.

late into the night, and saw how the .paople amused themselves. Just fancy it large plaza, or square, with a fair sprinkling of flowering trees, under which are fixed long tables,each finding room , for about a hundred. All the tables are full, and all: the people are gambling, men, women, and chill dren ; all, too, are smoking cigars, children as well. Strolling about are the prize fighters, with their gorgeous dresses, red shawls, and high felt hats. What a sight 1 Everybody gets supplied with cigars here, and all tame on board loaded with fruit and curios. We have now to spend a day watching the sharks, of which there are lots in the bay. I must now draw to a close, for my paper is done. If I can get none at the next port, Champerico, there will be no more writing until I get out of this beastly steerage. I cannot eat the salt horse they give us, so I am living on hard tack. I am pretty well through it all. November 27th, 1891.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE NEWLY DEPOSITED BILL.

- - - The Manchester Ship Canal Company have duly de- posited their Bill for next session lathe Private Bill Office of the House of Commons. Under this Bill, which con- tains 28 clauses and deals for the most part with the acquisition of additional lands, power is sought to abandon the works authorised in 1885 for the construe- tion of a dam and lock acrsse the river Mersey in the townships of Warrington and Walton Inferior' and to construct in lieu of those works a dam with a lock and sluices across the bed of the Mersey in a southerly direction commencing in Warrington about thirty- eight chains. east of the tiorthern end of Walton girder bridge and terrninatisg in Walton Inferior about forty-one chains east of the southern end of that bridge. The Company also ask leave to abandon at the southern end of Fairbrother-street, Salford, the opening bridge -across the river Irwell authorised in 1888, aticrthe Bill also proposes to repeal those sec- tions in the Act of 1885 which compel the company to complete the lock at Weston Point contemporaneously with the canal, and the works between "No Man's Land" and point " A " on the Parliamentary plan, in- chiding Weston Mersey lock,within two years after their commencement. An extension of time is also sought until the 31st December, 1895, for completing the War- rington dock, which is an extension of three years be- yond the time originally sanctioned. By clause 22 et the Bill Parliament will be asked to exempt all vessels entering or leaving the canal by the entrance channel at Eastham from the tolls, rates, or dues leviable by the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners under their Act of 187 e, and by clause 23 the company ask for power to demand a toll of 7s. ed. for every barge or tugboat proceeding along the Bridgewater Canal or the branch canals connected therewith and propelled by a power "other than animal power, such power being self-con- tained," Power is also sought by the company to claim and recover for conveyance of traffic over their railways such a portion of any through rate "as they would for the time being be authorised to charge in respect of the conveyance by them of that traffic over their railways." FRESH ARRANGEMENTS WII R ENGINEERS. _ .

It is stated that an important step in the administra- tion of the affairs of the Ship Canal has been decided upon by the Executive Committee. After the death of Mr. Walker, the directors of the company, in coming to a settlement with the trustees under Mr. Walker's will, continued in their service the engineers of each section of the canal, as well as those under the supreme control of Mr. Leader Williams, and the two sets of engineers thus became the servants of the Ship Canal Company. A notice to terminate their engagements has now been served upon the whole of the chief officials, with the exception of Mr. Leader Williams, and this notice is to expire on Marl 1 next. This will leave the executive committee with a free hand to complete the works by contract or otherwista, or to re-engage so many of the officials as they may deem necessary. Several of the sections of the canal are so far advanced that it will doubtless be considered the better plan to finish them out of hand with the company's own men, but in others an i entirely new contract will, it s believed, lead to a great saving in the estimated expenditure. The consideration of these steps will next engage the attention of the com- mittee.

div.head: SMALL FARMS OF FRANCE.
div.p: THE SMALL FARMS OF FRANCE.

The Rev. W. Tuckwell,our well-known friend the Radical parson, has paid a visit to France to study the condition of the small holders and villages. He brings back the usual cheerful report—that the French peasants are happy, contented, thrifty, and comfortable. He visited several places in the north- ern half of France, examined holdings near villages and met with "unbroken testimony" that "the pros- perity, freedom, and thrift of the labouring peasant is due to the facility of acquiring land at will and cheaply, consequent on the extinction of the great landlords at the Revolution." But, says the sham reformer, the division of the soil into small patches as in France is the ruin of agriculture. Nothing of the sort. "On the small farms, as on all other hold- ings we have seen," says Mr. Tuckwell, "the farm- ing was extraordinarily skilful. Not only was the land far cleaner than most farmers' in England—al- lotments at home had accustomed me to that—but w,.; were arrested by the dexterous economy in lay- ing out the crops, the unexected rotations and the use of chemical manures." This is the result of the agricultural education which has been carried on by the Government during the last ten years. France is now studded with agricultural colleges. schools, and scientific farms, where the peasants' sons are trained for next to nothing. Mr.Tuckwell's report will be found in this month's "Contempo- rary.'

div.head: WA RRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WA RRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
CONCERT AT THE PUBLIC HALL

'iThe second concert of the season, given by the Warrington Musical Society-was held in the Public Hall, on Tuesday, night. The concert was of an archestratcharacter, and was largely attended. The principal artistes were Mons. L., Dulonp, solo violin; Mr. F. W. Reynolds, solo pianoforte; and Madame , Clara Samuell, vocalist; Mr., Frank H. Crossley, as Lusual officiated as conductor, to whom must always I be awarded a meed of praise for the ability he dis- played in the discharge of his duties. On him, and to the orchestra generally,high encomiums ought to be bestowed for the manner in which the instru- mental,part of the concert passed off, the entertain- ment indeed constituting a rare treat. The over- ture, " Marionette," by Ourlitt, was succeeded by a violin -solo by Mons. Duloup, a Romance in F (Beeth- oven). A Hungarian dance (Brahms-Joachim), which was really splendidly executed, 1 the audience being so delighted that they would not content themselves with his returning to bow his thanks for their clamourous plaudits, but again recalled him, upon which he obliged with a mazurka by Wieuiawski. His violin solo, later on "Airs Russes" created an-even greater sensation, for after the performance he was recalled a third time, and to satisfy his inexorable auditors played Raff's well- known cavatina. An adagio for two violins by Bach, given by Mons. Duloup in -conjunction with Mr. F. H. Crossley, was a most careful and exquisite perform- ance, and was received with deserved applause. Mr. 'F. W. Reynolds played a concerto for the pianoforte and orchestra in D minor, by Mendelssohn, and at a later period of the evening, a Nocturne, by Chopin and a study, by Loeschorn, both pieces being execute, in a manner we have seldom heard surpassed, and the audience breaking out, especially on the latter being given, into enthusiastic applause, and compelling him on each occasion to come baCk and bow. Three songs— composed by Mr. Crossley, " Absence," " Restlessness," and" The evening sky; were sung by Madame Clara Samuel!, in a style which was almost faultless, the compass and modulation of her voice being strikingly excellent. She made a profound impression and received an almost uproarious encore, to which she responded with yet another song by the same composer. She also sang during the evening"' love my love "in a sur- passingly chatming manner and was recalled for this also, though in this instance, only complying so far as to bow. The concert concluded with a march" Cornelius," by Mendelssohn. The manner in which the Society's orchestra grappled with the difficulties of the " sym- phony" and the" concerto "deserves special mention, a nice balancing of the various instruments and a marked degree of precision and taste characterising the whole of its work.

div.head: LANCASHIRE, .DERBYSHIRE, AND EAST
div.p: LANCASHIRE, .DERBYSHIRE, AND EAST
COAST RAILWAY BILL.

The Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Rail- way Company have deposited their Bill for next session in the Private Bill Office of the House of Commons. Under this Bill, which contains 48 clauses, the company seek powers to construct about three miles of railway, the object of which is to connect their line authorised last session with the Clowne Colliery in Derbyshire, the Langwith Colliery in the same county,and the North Stafford- shire Railway at Prestbury. The company also ask Parliament to confirm an agreement with the North Sea Fisheries (East Lincolnshire) Harbour and Dock Company for the purchase of that under- taking by them for the sum of £lO,OOO, and in the event of this agreement being confirmed, the Bill provides for the winding up and dissolution of the Dock Company. The amount of additional capital sought to be raised under this Bill is less than £50,000, with £160,000 further borrowing powers, which, if sanctioned,will bring the total authorised share and loan capital of this cenipany up to £7,332,660. Power is, however,proposed to be con- ferred on the Great Eastern Railway Company to subscribe £250,000 towards this capital, and in res- pect of this subscription to have the right to ap• point one director on the board of the company. The company also seek power to enter into agree- ments with the Great Eastern Railway Company, the Great Northern and Great Eastern Joint Com- mittee, and London and North-Western Railway Company, the Midland, the North Staffordshire, and the Manchester, Sheffield,and Lincolnshire Railway Companies, or any of them, for working, managing, and Maintaining the railway. The Bill also pro- poses to confer running powers upon the Great Eastern Railway Company over the proposed new railways to the Clowne Colliery and:the Langwith Colliery.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO MR. LAWRENCE IRVING.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO MR. LAWRENCE IRVING.

Mr. Lawrence Irving the famous actor's second son, who accidentally shot himself in Belfast on Wednesday, spent a good night. Four medical men constantly attend him, but have not yet removed the bullet, which lodged behind the right lung. They, are, however hopeful of his recovery.
DEA.TH OF THE EARL OF LICHFIELD.

The Earl of Lichfield, whose life has been despaired of for sore days past, died on Thursday morning at Port- man-square, London. The deceased Earl was born in 1825, and was précis writer to Lord Palmerston when secretary for Foreign Affairs. He was a Liberal, and sat for Lichfield from 1847 to 1854. He is succeeded in his title by his eldest son, Viscount Anson. The cause of the Earl of Lichfield's death was paralysis,with which he was seized a fortnight since.

CIIAPTER AN rr,L-ASSORTED PAIR. -Lady Callerley might be as antagonistic as she 'chose in her own mind to her husband's nearest relative, but having nothing to rationally account for such a feeling, she was sensible enough to hold her peace about it, and to make no demur when Sir Lancelot proposed a walk over to Brearnish Hall on the following day. Besides, she was too glad of his company, and the excuse for them to be together, to throw any obstacle in the way. It was rather a long walk through the avenue and over the bridge, and Silvia, all unused to country walks, grew a trifle weary as they ascended, the last hill Sir Lancelot was very silent, and un- responsive, rso after awhile Lady Callerley's babyish chatter creased, and they went on side by side, without exchanging a word. At the top of the hill they halted, and looked down upon the Hall. A big, rambling house, with an ill-kept garden surrounding it on three sides; and an untidy farm- yard La the rear with pigs, poultry, and young beasts iruddled together in a slovenly and careless fashion, and a stackyard, telling more forcibly of a plentiful harvest the previous year than of any great skill on the farmer's part in the construction of stacks. Upon the gabled roof of the Hall, moss and house leek grew thickly, and flocks of pigeons sunned themselves, or rose into the air with flashes of prismatic hues. Two or three dogs of sporting breed, as setters and pointers, lay about the door; and welcomed the visitors with a series of barks and growls. It was a picturesque old place, but one which spoke of neglect and decay, of a careless master, and an indifferent mistress. Sir Lancelot and Sylvia ascended the moss-grown steps, the door was suddenly thrown open, and a noble boy of about, seven years of age ran out to

meet them. "Come in, Cousin Lancelot, and bring your wife with you! I know who you both are, though I've never seen you before, and besides, I heard them talking! Mother will be down directly. She's gone to change her gown, I suppose. Women are are always in such a fright if they are caught shabby, and she's been busy in the kitchen all the morning, though she'd be cross if she heard me tell you." "Upon my word you are a frank youngster," said Sir Lancelot laughing, and shaking hands with the lad, who looked up into his face with eyes exceedingly like his own in form and colour, though merrier in expression, as became one so young. He led them into a morning room, where the cold sunlight mercilessly showed up an ill-kept, faded sort of parlour, according well with the exterior of the house. "Welcome, Lady Callerley," exclaimed the boy, with pretty grace, and he drew forward a comfort- able chair, into which Silvia was not sorry to sink. She scanned the young face looking curiously into her own, trying to detect the mother in it, but forced immediately to acknowledge that she found no resemblance. She felt irresistibly at- tracted by the bright little lad, but she nevertheless was piqued to have to confess that it was her husband he resembled most. Little Lance re- turned her gaze with interest, and ventured nearer to her. "You are very pretty—just like a picture which hangs above my bed. The picture is ome of an angel whispering to a baby that is asleep, the angel is bigger than you, though; at least I think it would be, because its head reaches half way up the bed curtain, and yours wouldn't, you know! But I expected you to be little. My mother said you were— Here the boy suddenly stopped and flushed crimson. He was rather too prone to letting miscellaneous cats out of bags, and had a vivid memory of certain punishments, fitting this crime. "A chit of a schoolgirl" was the phrase he only just managed to shop short of. But in the place of feeling offended Silvia was charmed with his candour. She threw herself back in her chair, and burst into a merry peal of laughter, which even the entrance of Mrs. Breamish, sweet and composed and faultlessly -attired, could not alte- gether check. Mrs. Breamish looked slightly surprised, as she I shook hands with her guests. "Don't be alarmed, Dorothy," exclaimed Sir Lancelot, "it's only some fun your boy and my merry little wife are haying together." "I hope he has not been rude ?" asked Mrs. Breamish, with an uneasy glance at the culprit, who hung his head in a sheepish manner, though Silvia thought she detected a mischievous twinkle in the downcast eyes. "He is dreadfully spoilt, I'm afraid; but what can I do? His father will not take any trouble to correct him, and he is too big and self-willed for a woman to manage !" "Now that's too bad, mother—about daddy, I moan. You stopped him when he took his cane to me for tying old Riddell's wig and spectacles upon Towser when he was drunk—old Riddell, I mean, not Towser—and sending the dog in to his old woman, Mrs. Riddell that is, like that. Why did you not let him th lash me then, instead of screaming and going into hysterics at the very idea?" "It was a pity, but I will not be so lenient next time, I assure you, Lance. You see how ungrate- ful boys can be, Lady Callerley l" "I rather like boys, Mrs. Breamish. They are so truthful. But I daresay it is sometimes awkward to have them about !" Mrs. Breamish wondered if Silvia's naivette was real and assumed? It would be strange if such a young and seemingly simple creature should prove more than a match for herself in finesse and cleverness. But Dorothy Breamish had an immense belief in her own capabilities, so this musing did not trouble her long. The fact that all her cleverness had not made a success of her life did not daunt her. Cir- cumstances, not diplomacy, were to blame. Cir- cumstances it was that had given her nothing better than a stupid, drunken, spendthrift husband, and an encumbered estate, instead of the reverse of these. Had her cousin Lancelot only stayed at home when he was young and susceptible, instead of taking a sudden hatred to and a longing to escape from his native place, which longing he gratified immediately after his mother's death, why, there was no doubt he must have ended by caring for a cousin not devoid of charms, and one who took such pains to win his esteem and affec- tion. "Go and tell your father who is here, Lance, and see if you can induce him to leave his own snuggery and be polite to my kinsfolk," she re- quested, and the boy ran off at once. "Harry Breamish is more used to horses and dogs than to the society of town-bred ladies," she went on in a calm, soft tone, as though it were a stranger she referred to. "So I hope my new cousin will excuse any bluntness 'if speech, and seeming lack of courtesy in him ! He bath a good heart enough, but he is sadly lacking in the polish to which you are doubtless used, my dear Rilvia l" A mighty hubbo.b preceded the entrance of the master of the house: dogs barking, Master Lance laughing, and imitating the new hallo of the hunts- man dan hounds in full cry, and heart!, laughter at his precocious sporting tendencies echoing from his etre. I A big, ruddy-faced, jolly-looking man was Squire Breamish; though his thick blacCeyebrows, which he had a constant habit of contracting as he talked, gave the impression of a violent character, an im- pression borne out by his blustering manner. Yet people always found him more lenient and easier to deal with than his soft spoken wife. In fact, this manner seemed to a keen observer assumed to cover a consciousness of a certain adverse criticism he suffered from, and which helped to make him reckless and passionate. "Well, Callerley, you've come back to the North at last, and brought a young wife with you to help to settle you? Your servant, Lady Callerley I By Jupiter! Callerley, you've shown good taste and skill in choosing, though Madam here was by way of turning up her nose at your little pocket beauty. But, then, we all know what women are, eh? Let one be a bit prettier and younger than the rest 'and they'll all have a peck at her, and lead her a life like a speckled hen has among a lot o' black Spanish 'uns !' "Harry, my love Lady Callerley is from Court, and your language may sound a little— well, a little homely in her ears," expostulated Mrs. Breamish, in mellifluous tones. But her cold grey eyes rested on the speaker, and he grew dis- tinctly uncomfortable under their gaze. His face flushed and the veins on his forehead swelled. Years of matrimonial experience had taught him the subtle irony which could be hidden in the sweetest of voices. And if there was -ett aleinq more than another the squire detested /n-. 1 it was the idea of appearing ridiculous. He turned to Silvia uneasy and self-conscious. parclen..l44v Callerley ; I'm in the rough.
