officially of the increase of sulphur in the gas. If they had a testing apparatus at the Town Hall he did not think it could be much used, but they had one at the Gas Works and any member of the Cauncil could see it there.

The MAYOR said Dr. Gornall was asked to look after the apparatus at the Town Hall, but he did not know whether he had done so or not. Alderman Holmes would bring the matter before the next meeting of the Gas Committee.
The minutes wore then confirmed. THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY AND WARRINGTON.— THE UPPER MERSEY NAVIGATION COMMISSION.

The Rivers Committee recommended that the Borough Suveyor be instructed to make a report upon the Man- chester Ship Canal Bill, with detail drawings and sec- tions of the proposed works so far as they affect this borough ; and that Joseph Davies, Esq., be reappointed to represent the Corporation on the Upper Mersey Navi- gation Commission for the further term of three years, and that the common seal of the borough be affixed to the necessary deed of appointment. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH, in moving the confirma- tion ofithe minutes, said they. had asked the borough surveyor to make his report m order to safeguard the interests of the Corporation in regard to the Ship Canal. Councillor MONKS seconded.

Councillor H. ROBERTS supported the minutes. He hoped it was the letermination of the Council at this most critical period of the construction of the Ship Canal that the interests of Warrington shquld be de- fended by the best ability that could be obtained for the purpose. If they were right in their understanding of the Bill it seemed clear that the Corporation of Manches- ter wanted to drop the construction of the docks in Arpley fields. If that was their intention, they must fight against it, and he hoped they should not hesitate to spend whatever money might be necessary to insist upon the faithful carrying out of the pledges incorpo- rated in Acts of Parliament. The interests of Warring- ton were at that moment in a state of very great crisis, and he was sure the Council would support the Rivers Committee in whatever action they might deem desir- able in the interests of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS said it appeared to him that any- thing with reference to the Bill in Parliament should have been given.to the Parliamentary Sub-Committee. If the Ship Canal Company threw Warrington over,what then? Councillor FLEMING : Ruin. Alderman BURGESS: Not quite, as long as we have so many tanneries. (Laughter.) He did not think it would be so terrible a thing. He thought it vveuld be found that a syndicate would be formed at Warrington which would construct the docks for the town, and which would have the full benefits of them instead of the Ship Canal Company having any of them. He also referred to the appointment of their esteemed friead, Mr. Davies, to represent the Corporation on the Upper Mersey Corn- mission, and suggested that it would be much better for , some one to be appointed who was still a member of the Council. He thought either of the Messrs. Fairclough were well adapted for the appointment, and suggested that the recommendation should be taken back and re- considered. Councillor FAlRcLouGu,as Chairman of the Committee, expressed his willingness ta withdraw the recommenda- tion as to the appointment of Mr. Davies. Councillor FLOOD thought Alderman Burgess was inconsistent in this position, inasmuch as he voted for the appointment of Major Pickmere, who was not a member of the Council, as a representative trustee of the Grammar School. Councillor GREENING defended the action of the Com- mittee in regard to the Ship Canal, but said he agreed with Alderman Burgess as to the proposed appointment of Mr. Davies. Councillor BOLTON moved that the appointment of Mr. Davies be confirmed. Councillor FLOOD seconded. Councillor HEATON said it ought to be understood in future that any position in connection with the Council should be held by-members of the Council .Councillor F. A. ROBERTS supported the appointment

of Mr. Davies. _ _ Councillor H. Romirrrs agreed with the soggestion of Mr. Heaton. He pointed out that these appointments had been made with the express object of giving local authorities a direct representation upon those outside authorities. In the appointment of Major Pickmere they made a grievous mistake, as they had now only one- third—Alderman Harrison—of the direct representation they should have among the trustees of the Grammar School. That was not a question of giving honour to Mr. Davies, but it was a question of their retaining those appointments in the hands of men directly con- nected with the Council. (Hear, hear.) He also de- fended the action of the Committee in regard to the Ship Canal scheme. Councillor DIXON thought a member of the Council should be appointed in the place of Mr. Davies, while Councillor flurcnissox argued in favour of Councillor Bolton's amendment.

For the amendment there voted Alderman Wright, Councillors Bolton, Smethurst, Hill, Muir, Ashton, Hutchinson, Flood, F. A. Roberts, and Heaton-10. Against the amendment : Aldermen Burgess, Holmes ; Councillors Bonne 11, Blackhurst, Fairclough, H. Roberts, Plumpton, Greening, Dixon, Fleming, R. T. Fairclough, Shaw-Green, Cannell, Beaman, Br)wne, and Monks-16. , The amendment was therefore carried and the minutes as altered were passed.

THE FIRE STATION. The Fire Engine Committee reported that the borough treasurer had been instructed to forward an account to Mr. W. Gill, Bridge-st., for £1 7s. 6d., in connection with the fire on his premises. It had also been resolved that the Watch Committee be requested to have the police office connected with the telephone exchange; and that the Watch Committee be asked to place a hydrant in the yard at the fire engine station. Councillor HUTCHINSON moved, and Councillor HEA- TON seconded, that the minutes be confirmed. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOMIL suggested that if the new barracks were purchased by the Corporation it would be a suitable place for the firemen all living near together. The minutes were confirmed. THE WATER RATES. _

The Water Committee's minutes contained the follow- ing resolutions ; That the following recommendations of the Managing Sub-Committee be adopted :-1, That the property of the undertaking be insured ; 2, that, on the request of the Fire Engine Committee, new and im- proved hydrants be placed in Bridge-at. •, 3, that a plan showing all water-pipes and mains, and also an estate plan, be prepared and placed in the office. That, after the 29th September, 1892, the :water rates be collected half-yearly, on the 25th March, and the 29th September in each year. The DEPUTY-MAYOR moved, and Alderman WRIGHT seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON complained of the alteration in the time for collecting the water rates, and said that to many small property owners, members of building societies and others, the present time of collection was much more convenient. Councillor SHAW-GREEN said the change was absolutely necessary to fall in with the municipal year,which ended with the 31st of March. Councillor MONKS asked if the new hydrants were to be fixed' on the Appleton or the Winwick supply. The DRPUTY-MAYOR : On the Winwick supply. The minutes were confirmed.
THE PROPOSED PURCHASE OF THE OLD BARRACKS,

NOT AGREED TO. . The principal recommendations in the minutes of the General Purposes Committee were that the militia store- house and premises in Wilson Patten-street, Warring to n, be purchased from the County Council of Lancashire for the sum of £4,750 ; and that the Town Clerk be

instructed to apply to the Local Government Board for permission to borrow the said sum of £4,750, and also the sum of £4,100 for the purchase of the premises at Market Gate, and the sum of £4,500 for the purchase of the premises at Bridge Foot which have recently been acquired by the Corporation. The DEPUTY MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BLACHHURST, in seconding, recapitulated the negotiations for the purchase of the old barracks as set forth in the letter given in our columns last week. He remarked that it had been the feeling of the Markets Committee that they should clear the streets of the animal fairs, and, more, that it was probable that even- tually the Board of Agriculture would eventually call upon them to remove the fairs and find some other suit- able place. If they were called upon suddenly to find another place it would cost them a vast amount of money. The Committee thought this property would answer their purpose for some few years to come, and if it were not all they could desire for the fairs it could be handed over amongst other purposes to the Sanitary Committee for their vans, &c. If the Council rejectea the recommendations they would put the Markets Com- mittee in a very difficult position. Councillor Cianexu. moved as an amendment that the recommendation with regard to the purchase of the old barracks be referred back. He considered the place was not fit for a fair or market, and he held it was simply senseless waste of money at the present time. (Hear, hear, and "No, no.") Councillor DIXON seconded the amendment, and remarked that at other towns the fairs were being taken out of the towns altogether. He was sure plenty of land could be got for lass money for that purpose. Counciller Bourow also opposed the purchase. He did not think that Council should become property owners. Councillor Boxxecr. thought it was a ridiculou3 thing to attempt to purchase the barracks, and he suggested that more suitable land might be got in Dallam-lane or Longford-street. Alderman WRIGHT said that unless a better case was made out by Councillor Blackhurst he could not see his way to support the purchase. He did not say the pro- perty was dear at first sight, but if they did not want it, it was dear at any price. He understood that the whole income from the fairs during the past year was only £l5 or £l6. He did not think that Corporation should be the owners of sanitary property, and he thought their medical officer would soon tell them the cottages at the barracks were insanitary. Alderman BURGESS said the Council appeared disposed to fritter away in small sums money which vvould be required before long for serious purposes. (A Voice : Longford.) Let him tell that gentleman that Longford was the only place that brought money in, and if they could show him that that other place would approach within miles miles of Longford,he should be rather more inclined to support the purchase. (Oh, Oh, and laugh- ter.) He suggested that they should do the wise thing and abolish altogether the fare charges. Ho opposed the purchase of the barracks. Councillor SHAW GREEN referred to the necessity there would soon be for providing suitable places for fairs and cattle sales, and added that the barracks could at a slight cast be made eminently suitable for the purposes of the Technical Instruction Committee. There were 7,000 yards of land at the barracks, and this alone at 6d. per yard would come to £3,500. They could afford to make the purchase out of revenue without taxing the borough at all. One of their ma!istrates had remarked tc. him that the barracks would be most serviceable as a police court, and there were all possible conveniences on the spot for that purpose. Councillor FLEMING supported the proposal of the Markets Committee. The Council might, he said, put up industrial dwellings. It was a most desirable bargain. Councillor HEATON said a cattle market was not re- quired at the end of the town. From the very day on which the barracks were built they had not returned a fraction of the outlay. They were not at all suitable for anything the Corporation wanted, and the cottages there were not in accordance with their bye-laws. Councillor HUTCHESON believed it would be a ridiculous purchase and would not pay its way. He suggested that they might get land within 300 yards of Warrington Bridge at lid. per yard suitable for a fair around. Councillor H. ROBEETS suggested that the minute should be referred back for further consideration. He said the barracks could be put to several important important uses, and if the Council did not secure the property,aomebody not very far out of the Council would not improbably purchase it before the week was out, and a good deal of the opposition that night was, per- haps, not quite so straightforward as it might be. Alderman WRIGHT : That is rather serious. Councillor BOLTON: I hope you don't mean that Alderman Burgess is going to purchase it. (Laughter.) Councillor WRIGHT : I am not aware of anything of the kind.

Councillor RolmTs said he was speaking with a little knowledge that had been conveyed to him in a way some people might not suspect. He knew there were people prepared to pay £5,000 for the property the very next day. A MEMBER : Let them do it, then: Th. DEPUTY-MAYOR: I think it is a bogus rumour; I have heard the same thine. Councillor ROBERTS did not think it was.

Alderman BURGESS: Vote, vote. Councillor ROBERTS said if there was one gentleman who, more than another had occupied the time of the Council that night, it was Alderman Burgess. Alderman BURGESS: And he occupied it exceedingly well. .

Councillor FLEMING : Nothing like blowing your own trumpet. Councillor ROBERTS : That is entirely a matter of opinion. Alderman BURGESS : No; there is a great concensus of opinion. Councillor ROBERTS: There is always a great consen - SuS of opinion centred in Alderman Burgess. (Laughter.) Why, he added, were the publicans so active in opposing that purchase? Councilior CANNELL said he came there simply to say it was a senseless scheme ; he was not connected with the publicans in any way. Councillor ROBERTS said there was a French proverb which said that a man who excused himself accused himself. (Laughter.) He left that for adaptation by gentlemen concerned. Councillor CANNELL : I deny I -am connected with the publicans. The DEPUTY-MAYOR : Councillor Roberts did not say

to. Councillor ROBERTS : My friend protests too much. Councillor CANNRLL : I shall have the last word if he gets on that subject. Councillor ROBERTS, continuing, said there had been a scheme for the concentration of the various departments of the Corporation at the Town Hall, and he pointed out that in that case they would need another place for the stables. He agreed that the barracks were not big enough for the half-yearly cattle fairs, but he contended that, at any rate, the purchase proposal deserved , further consideration by the General Purposes Com- mittee. (Hear, hear.) Councillor GREENING supported the suggestion of Councillor Roberts. The DEPUTY-MAYOR asked Councillor Cannell if he would withdraw his amendment. Councillor CANNELL : Vote. A vote was then taken as follows :—For the amend- ment : The Deputy-Mayor ; Aldermen Burgess and Wright ; Councillors Bonnell, Fleaton, Dixon, F. A. Roberts, Hutchinson, Ashton. Muir, Beaman, Smethurst, Hill, Cannell, and Bolton-15. Against the amendment : Councillors Monks, Black- hurst, J. Fairclough, Flood, Plumpton, Browne, Shaw Green, R. T. Fairclough, Greening, H. Robtrts, and Fleming-11.

div.head: amendment being carried, the proposed purchase of the barracks was, of course, rejected. INSANITARY HOUSES.—PROPOSED INIPROVENIENT
div.p: The amendment being carried, the proposed purchase of the barracks was, of course, rejected. INSANITARY HOUSES.—PROPOSED INIPROVENIENT

SCHEME. The Sanitary Committee's minutes contained the fol- lowing recommendations :—That the tender of Mr. Thos. Pilkington to provide horses and drivers at 7s. per day be accepted ; that the sum of £lO be allowed to Mr. Thos. Pllkington for the services of horse and man at the embankment at Longford depot; that Mr. Joseph Taylor be appointed an agent of the Corporation for the sale of concentrated manure upon the same terms as those upon which the other agents of the Corporation are appointed; that a license be granted to Mr. Frank Connolly for the use and occupation of a slaughter-house in Morris's-yard Church-street, for the 12 months commencing Ist Jan., 1892. The minutes also contained the resolution with regard to the insanitary property near Dial-st. which we published last week. Alderman BURGESS, in moving the adoption of the minutes' said that there was one subject on the agenda paper of the very greatest importance, and which would require the most careful consideration of the committee, and of the Council, before anything was done in the, matter. It was a subject which might involve the ex-i penditure of thousands of pounds of the ratepayers' money. He thought it was hardly necessary for him to make any other reference than to the Medical Officer of Health's reports. They were of such a character that it was necessary that they should be considered to some extent that evening. The committee wished to take the Council into their confluence, in order that they might be guided in the course necessary to be adopted, and to ascertain if the proposals on the agenda paper accorded with their views. He then read the following extract from the report book of the Medical Officer of Health, December 9, 1891 :—" Insaiiitary pro- perty. On the 7th January I brought under your notice under part I. of the Act known as the Housing of the Working Classes, 1890, an official representation of the unhealthiness of a district situated in St. John's Ward; and bounded by Dial-st., Fennel-st., and Cockhedge,, and a Hee drawn from north to south, from 60 Cock. hedge-lane, to 12, Dial-st. the unhealthiness is in the main due to (a) houses, courts, and alleys, being unfit for human habitation ; (b) to the narrowness, closeness, , and bad arrangement, and bad condition of the streets and houses within the area ; the want of light, air, and ventilation, Ste. After an extended knowledge of these lacts, I felt satisfied that these sanitary defects in such area could not be effectually remedied otherwise than by an improvement scheme for the re-arrangement and re-construction of the streets and houses within such area. I desire, therefore (as no decided legal action has been taken), to withdraw entirely my certificate of the 28th May, 1891, to deal with a number of the houses en- closed within the said area under Part 11. of the same Act, and to adhere to my report of the 7th January. I must inform you that under the terms of my appoint- ment as Medical Officer of Health, it is my duty to in- form the Local Government Board that I have presented such a report dealing with an insanitary area as that of the 7th Janua.y.—(Signed) JonN H. GORNALL." As the Sanitary Committee had adopted the resolutions set forth on the agendar, it was only fair that he (Aid. Burgess) should state there was no antagonism between the doctor and the committee. The Committee felt that it would be an improper thing to allow so important a work to be carried out unless the nature of it had been thoroughly examined. Alderman Burgess then proceeded to read the following report, which was submitted by the Medical Officer of Health to the members of the Sanitary Committee, on January 7, 1891 :—" Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1890. Under this Act I beg to make the following representation : That within the area bounded by Dial-street on the south, by dwellings numbered 12 to 44 alternately ; on the east by Fennel- street, by houses numbered 16 to 50 ; on the north by Cocishedge-lane, by houses numbered from 60 to 82 ' • and on the west by a line drawn from north to south, from 60, Cockhedge-lane to 12, Dial-street, are houses, courts, alleys, the narrowness, closeness, and bad arrangement of which, together with want of sufficient light, air, and ventilation, are dangerous and injurious to the health of the inhabitants of the buildings in the', said area. This area contains 12,557 square yards, or a little over 4 acres, and at the present time ' the population numbers 619 persons, or about 250 persons to an acre, whilst the density of the population of the borough is only 34 to an acre. The death rate of this area, for the year 1890, is above 40 per 1,000 of the population, whilst that of the borough will be about 22.5 per 1,000. Though I mention the three streets,&c., ' as boundaries,it is not with the intention of condemning all the houses included in them as insanitary, but for the purpose of description and convenience, for under Section VI., under any scheme adopted, you may ex- clude any part of an area in respect of which an official representation is made, &c. The yards and courts in this area demanding your attention are—Dial-yard,Rose- yard, Back Rose-yard, Filling's-court, Webster's-yard, Green's-court, Fennel-st., Vernon's-yard, Pritchard's- yard , Robinson's-yard, Pilkington's-yard,Garner's-brow, Cockhedge, Dial-court, Cockhedge. Some few houses are very dilapidated, many are approached by narrow covered passages, a great many are back-to-back houses. Some can be abolished as separate tenements, and their , rooms added to the houses behind them, thus forming two back-to-back houses into one through house." The Medical Officer's report gave a list of houses, which were in a state so dangerous or injurious to health as to be unfit for habitation, and the whole of the houses enu- merated in the doctor's list had been disposed of with one exception, and that was the property of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., viz. No. 3, Say-horse yard, Foundry-st. It was only right, however, to mention that these gentlemen were quite prepared to make any improvements which the Town Council wanted. The importance of this subject was so great, that he did not think it would be found that the scheme admitted the taking down of a portion of the district, allowing the rest to stand. If the scheme was sanctioned by the Local Government Board, bethought that they would have to obtain a small Act of Parliament—a small Act and not an expensive matter. He thought that they would have to acquire the whole area. There was no other alternative, and that meant the purchase of over 100 houses. In the area there was a manufacturing pro- perty known as the Dial Mills ; whether these would have to be removed or not he was not prepared to say. It would perhaps cost-- Councillor FLEIVIING : £lOO,OOO. Alderman Buie:Ass said it would not cost that snm nor £30,000. The purchase would be effected by arbitration He thought that they ought to first know whether the area was in a condition which did not admit of its being improved. (Hear, hear.) If it was in the condition which their Medical Officer of Health stated it to be, they were bound to deal with it. They should have every house visited, and a proper examination made from one end ot the district to the other. On June 2, 1891, the Medical Officer of Health furnished the Saul- Committee with a list of a large number of houses which he declaredl were unfit for habitation' and the Town Council confirmed the proceedings of the committee in reference to those houses. In answer to the notices which were served by the Town Clerk, all, or in nearly every case, the owners of the property came, and said that they were prepared to do what the Town Council considered necessary to place the homes compained of in a proper condition for habitation. There did not appear to be any great hurry to move in the matter. An ap- plication would have to be made in Parliament in Nov- ember next. There was time, therefore, to obtain all the information required. Alderman SUTTON seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor FLEMING said that this question seemed to be a very serious one. He thought that the area was in an insanitary condition, and after the recume which had been given by Alderman Burgess he was more than ever convinced that the district was in a very bad condition. He was not one of those who advocated demolition of

property. The scheme might cost £lOO,OOO. Someone had said £20,000. He wished to know in the case of insanitary dwellings ir. class HI., could they he des- troyed without the'ownera obtaining compensation or what compensation they would get. Alderman BURGESS said that compensation would he awarded by arbitration. Councillor FLEMING said that in the cases of houses de- clared to be unfit for habitation, provided they were made habitable, he would be inclined to let them stand. Councillor BROWNS said that they would not require an Act of Parliament to deal with this area. They would only have to obtain a provisional order from the Local Government Board. Alderman BURGESS : It IS the same thing. Councillor BROWNS said the Act under which they were moving was one of the most stringent Acts that had ever been passed. and practically compelled the Sanitary Authority to carry out what the medical officer

reported. Councillor BOLTON wished to be informed if houses that were in a satisfactory condition to the Medical Officer of Health in the proscribed area would have to be pulled down. (" No, no.") What he wanted to know was whether a house which was in a satisfac- tory condition would be left alone. No one pre- sent seemed to know much about the matter. The doctor was infallible, and was going to do everything. Alderman BURGESS replied that he was advised that if the scheme was sanctioned, every building on the area mentioned would have to be cleared off. Councillor BOLTON : Houses of all classes? Councillor FLEMING : Including the Rose and Crown. (Loud laughter.) Alderman FRANCOMB : That will be put in Fennel-

strTeT(fiWJ,Wdi-a-t.ighter.) Councillor Dixott' alluded to a fine which had been in- flicted by the committee on Messrs. N. Greening and Sons, Limited, for emitting dense smoke. Councillor BOLTON: lam glad to hear that. (Laugh- ter.) Councillor DIXON complained that while other manu- facturers were fined, those making iron could not be touched. Alderman SUTTON advised Councillor Dixon to make those complaints to the Legislature, and not to the Sanitary Committee, as the committee were compelled to carry out the law as it was. Councillor Musa asked if a house were condemned by the Medical Officer, would the Council permit it to be tenanted if the owners put it into proper condition? Councillor H. ROBERTS pointed out that at the present moment there was no scheme before the Council for consideration, and the object of the resolution pro- posed was to obtain information necessary to guide the Sanitary Committee. The committee wanted to know before they submitted any scheme to the Council involv- ing an expenditure of money, whether any appreciable portion of the property was capable of improvement, so that it might be done by the owners of the property, and not at the expense of the ratepayers. They had a duty to perform to the people who inhabited these houses, as well as to the ratepayers of Warrington. Upon the Sanitary Committee devolved the duty of seeing that no man or woman should live in property that was unfit for habitation. Ile felt certain that the Town Council would rise to the importance of the oscasion, and emul- ate the example which nad been set by other towns in this respect, and that they would see that the poor had proper dwellings to live in. Alderman BURGESS said he was of opinion that they should have an analysis of the death rate, in order to allow them to judge to what extent these dwellings were responsible, or whether the deaths were due in a greater measure to the habits of the people. Councillor BLACIIIIIIRST Are you going to make the' landlords responsible for the dirty habits of the people. The minutes were then carried. CORPORATION CONTRACTS.—LIVELY DISCUSSION —A MOTION "KICKED OUT."

-- Councillor HILL moved the following resolution of which he bad given notice i--" That all tenders for work, or estimates or contracts for the same, be sent in envelopes supplied by the firm or person who send the estimates or contracts, and not in those supplied by the Corporation, and be opened by the Chairman of the Committee to whom they are addressed." He said the matter did not interest him in the least, but he believed that if the motion were passed it would give satisfaction to tradesmen in the town. CouncillorCANNELL seconded the motion. Councillor BOLTON supported the motion. If there was any suspicion of envelopes being opened he thought it should be done away with. Alderman BURGESS said he could not support the motion. He did not know that anything had ever taken place to which the motion referred. He thought that before they accepted a resolution of that sort Mr. Hill, the mover of it, should give an explanation. So far as the Sanitary Committee was concerned, tenders which came there were regularly opened by whoever was in the chair at the meeting. He had never had the slightest reason to suppose that in some office in that building— for that was what the motion amounted to—tenders were opened and particulars given to other people ten- dering, that they might alter their tenders. He did not believe that had ever taken place or ever would take place. If Mr. Hill had reason to believe it did, let him disclose his information. (Hear, hear.) The DEPUTY-MAYOR said it was only the raving and Sewerage Committee that used those envelopes and if the chairman of that Committee would agree to pass a resolution on his own Committee that in future no printed envelopes shall be used there was an end of the matter. He himself had never seen a single envelope opened except in Committee by the chairman or some one whom the chairman has asked to assist him. Of course some people would always, be suspicious if they did not get a contract. Alderman WRIGITT said he represented a Committee that saw more of those tenders than any other, and he felt keenly for Mr. Longdin, and unless Couneillor Hill showed some good cause why he brought forward that resolution he should not ask his Committee to make any change whatever. (Hear, hear.) They found those en- velopes to be most convenient for tenders. He did net see anything to be gained by passing such a resolution, and he was sorry it had been brought forward. If Coun- cillor Hill could make any specific charge against the borough surveyor or an official of that Corporation he should be one of the first to see it bottomed. Councillor BRow/krs said he hoped the Council would vote against the resolution. If a than brouttlit a resolu- tion like that before the Council and did not prove enough to give a meaning to it, it was a gross slander either upon the borough surveyor, the chairman of a committee, or somebody else. (Hear, hear.) Councillor H. ROBERTS said he rose to speak as strongly as it was in his power to speak against both the manner and character of that resolution. If Councillor Hill meant what was conveyed in that resolution he inferen- tially slandered in the most disgusting and abominable manner the character of one of the chief officials of that Corporation. (Hear, hear.) The suggestion in the reso- lution was that tenders when they were sent in were tampered with by the horough surveyor acting in collusion with some party anxiousto tender to the Cor- poration. Councillor CARRELL: It does not say so. Councillor ROBERTS.: There are other ways of killing a cat besides poisoning it. He thought those who drew up the resolutton should have had the assistance of a 6th or 7th standard boy from the Peoples' College. It was about as ungrammatical as it could be— Councillor CARRELL : That is the Town Clerk's fault. The Tows CLERK said it was published exactly as be got it. Councillor ROBERTS said it was a mean unmanly thing to suggest by inference that the Borough Surveyor was capable of doing what was suggested by the resolution. Councillor CANNEL', : Nothing of the kind. Councillor ROBERTS : What else do you mean if you do not mean that the Borough Surveyor is capable of doing this sort of thing. If you believe that the Borough Surveyor is acting honourably what on earth is the necessity of such a resolution ? Covncillor CANNELL : Why do you object. Councillor ROBE RTS : The borough surueyor does not

object. Alderman WRIGHT I object. Councillor ROBERTS said the borough surveyor's mouth was closed, hence the extra meanness of the re- solution. They were taking advantage of the dafence- less position Mr. Longdin was in seeing he was not a member of that respectable body. What Englishmen liked more than another was fairplay. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Roberts then pointed out that similar envelopes were used for their tenders by other public bodies and he mentioned the Mersey Docks and Harbours Board. He hoped the Council would kick the resolution out as it deserved to be. Mr. BILL repudiated the remarks of Councillor Roberts and said he had great respect for the borough surveyer. Councillor Boman : You have a funny way of show- ing it. A vote was then taken and as only Councillors Hill, Cannel]. and Bolton voted for the motion it was rejected bra large majority. The meeting then ended, the Council having sat from six o'clock to 9.15

POLITICIANS, and general readers Pitt by with a taste for biography, have a Lord Rosebery. treat before them if they have not yet read Lord ROSEBERY'S volume on WILLIAM PITT, in the English Statesmen series published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. It is as entertaining as a first-class novel,and exceedingly instructive as a statesman's review of the life and conduct of statesmen. PITT, as the son of the great Earl of Chatham,seldom has justice done to him by Liberal writers, for his name is associated with the war with Napoleon and the piling up of hundreds of millions of our National Debt. Even Byron seems to have had a grudge against him whilst paying him a compliment, for he says : • Pitt, too, had his pride, And as a high-souled Alinister of State is Renowned for ruining Great Britain gratis.

Yet nothing is more certain, now that all tho facts are made known, than that PITT as Prime Minister steadfastly shut his eyes, as long as he could,to the proceedings of the Revolutionists in France, and it was only when treaties were being set aside and this country was threatened that he resorted to war—war which he afterwards prosecuted,as he was in duty bound, with all the energy of which he was capable. Having regard to the troubled condition of Ireland during this long continental war, it is not too much to say that England never passed through a greater crisis; and that she passed ' through without such internal convulsion as tore France asunder was undoubtedly due to the cour- age and genius of the great commoner who ruled the land for an unbroken period of seventeen years. It is perhaps useless to speculate on how much different and better it would have been for England if PITT had been at liberty to pursue the policy which he originally laid down of promoting trade and establishing a sound system of finance ; but it is due to his memory to declare that these things were dear to his heart. In view of all that has been heard of the policy of "three acres and a cow," and all that is now being heard upon social and industrial questions, it is of special interest to read the following account which Lord Rosebery gives of a scheme which PITT had for improving the condition of the poor. After referring to PITT'S speech in the House of Commons on the subject, he says:—

II 7 He followed it up with a Bill, full of novel and comprehensive propositions; so novel and compre- hensive,indeed,that,after several alterations, it sank over-weighted beneath the parliamentary wave. A vast new system was to be created ; a hierarchy of Justices and Wardens and Guardians, in every parish or group of parishes were to be established Schools of Industry, which were in fact what we have since known as Ateliers Nationaux. Their conditions were to he settled to some extent by Parish Councils; but they were in all cases to fur-

nish work for the destitute poor. The Justices and. other authorities were to have nearly the powers of a private employer of labour with regard to them. They were to buy materials ; they were to sell the manufactured article; they were to fix the rate of wages. They could build or hire warehouses; they could buy or hire land. They could enclose and cultivate commons for the support of the workers i in the Schools of Industry. Moreover, n every parish or union, a friendly society was to be estab- lished. Persons also, having more than two cbild- ren, or, in case of a widow, one child, were entitled to claim exceptional relief. A certain amount of visible property was not to debar a person from receiving parochial aid. There were, indeed, some 130 clauses more or less. One—perhaps the most daring in those days— provided that money 1141 be advanced, in deserving cases, for the purchase 0 a cow or some other animal producing profit. tham, in his criticisms on the measure, urged that a cow required three acres of grass, and 95Y341 whence these were to come. Though the ques.t_ilen was not answered, the proposal will be recogmst"' as the germ of a proverbial policy. As showing how little there is new under the sun, it may be remarked that the Duke of RIO" moNn of those days advocated annual Parliaments and manhood suffrage. Pur himself saw and ad,. mitted that the hereditary principle of rule won.' not stand the test of time, for he remarked'" whilst in France in 1783—just before his accession to power—that, "The part of our constitution whim will first perish is the prerogative of tilt: King and the authority of the House of Poeta. Such views may be said to be those of a Liberal rather than a Whig, for, as Lord ROSEDERY SaYS; " The Whig creed lay in a triple divine righV the divine right of the Whig families ta govern the Empire; to be maintained by the Empire; to prove their superiority by humblinf and bullying the Sovereign of the )3 nipire• This is neatly stated, and the book abounds .0 similar epigrammatic summaries, such, for 21/1: stance, as the reference to the bribery by laic' the union with Ireland was accomplished in 10' Thus "The corruption was black, hideats.l horrible ; revolting at any time, atrocious vvhen is remembered that it was a nation's birthright that was being sold." It is a redeeming feature, that PITT personally kept his hands clean, ow believing this, the reader will be disposed to eei with Lord ROSEBERY, in concluding the work' "There may have been men both able and greater than he, though it is not easy to cite the'' ; bC in all history there is no more patriotic sPillt" none more intrepid, and none more pure."

It is being suggested that, if the Ship Canal Company raise a difficulty about making the pro- mised dock for Warrington, the dock scheme should be taken up and carried out by a Syndicate, or by the Corporation. But the right course is to hold the Canal Company to their engagement; and, if need be, fight them tooth and nail on the point. There will be no difficulty about showing the Parliamentary Committee that a dock is a necessity for Warrington, that it was part of the original plan, and that not to make a dock would constitute a case of having obtained money under false pretences so far as Warrington shareholders are concerned. Besides, a separate Company, or the Corporation,would be more or less in the hands of the Ship Canal Company, who would be in a position to dictate terms. No ; a bargain is a bar- gain, and should be fairly carried out.

div.p: MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN:

, The annual tea party and entertainment took place on Tuesday evening at the Seamen's Institute. About 200 sat down to an excellent tea, over 100 sailors and flatmen being invited free. I pleasant and enjoyable evening was spent. On Wednesday the boat children's tea party and Christmas tree took place, and the young people thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

div.head: LIVERMORE BROS. COI7RT MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LIVERMORE BROS. COI7RT MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN.

This celebrated troupe of minstrels pay a visit to Run- corn next week, when they will occupy the Public Hall on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday evenings. A new and novel programme will be presented. Besides ballads, songs, burlesques, Szc., there have been engaged The Lentos, champion one-wheel bicyclists, and Trillo, the marvellous ventriloquist. A night of unalloyed enjoy- ment is promised. & W. DUTTON'S ANNUAL WINTER SALE is now on Sankey-Bt.—Advt.

DYSON'S DIOARAMA. AND GIPSY CHOIR AT RUNCORN. This well known and popular combination paid a visit to Runcorn this week, after an absence of five vears,and they have been welcomed by good audiences each even- ing. The diorama is of unusual excellence, the pictures possessing much artistic merit, and anyone witnessing the whole course with Mr. Dyson for guide, would know more about the beauties of his native laud and of foreign countries than he knew before. The vocal and instru- mental music is also well worth listening to, and there is not a dull moment in the whole entertainment.

FUNERAL OF MISS COOK, OF RUNCORN. The Mortal remains of Miss Mary Jane Cook, eldest daughter of Mr. Thomas Cook, Church-st., and mistress of (I renville-st. Infant School, wore interred in Runcorn Cemetery,on Tuesday afternoon,the officiating ministers being the Rev. T. Wilkes and the Rev. W. Arrowsmith. The deceased, who had succumbed to a lingering illness on Thursday, was followed to her last resting-place by a large number of mourners. Her premature decease is mourned by a large number of friends, who deeply sym- pathise with her parents in their sad bereavement. GA.S FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Cias Fitter, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO •PONKEY,

Before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. Brundrit, at Run- I corn Police Court, on Thursday, John Bright was charged with having cruelly ill-treated a donkey, the property of Mrs. Cardoss, at Halton, on the 26th December last.— The evidence for the prosecution showed that as the plaintiff's son was driving the donkey and cart down Halton-rd., the prisoner jumped on the animal's bait causing it to fall down apd break its knees, besides sus- taining ether injuries—Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, who defended, did not deny the facts, but contended that there was no wilful ill-treatment. It was a foolish joke by the prisoner, who immediately after the accident, expressed his regret and offered to pay for the damage.— The Bench took this view of the case and discharged th:3 prisoner.

div.head: THIEF WELL CAUGHT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A THIEF WELL CAUGHT AT RUNCORN.

James Murphy, a stranger, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Tuesday, charged with stealing a pair of boots, belonging to Thomas Whinyats, Church- 1 st., and a pair of trowsers, the property of Arnold Uns- worth, High-st. On Monday, P.C. Woolley and P.C. Edwards watched the prisoner take the boots from the shop door, and the prisoner seeing the officers, dropped the boots on the pavement, and walked into the shop, where he asked for a pair of shoes. He was asked by the officers to produee his money for the pnrchase,and it was i found that he had not a penny n his possession. As Mr. Whinyats would not prosecute, the prisoner was allowed to go. Later in the day he committed the theft at Mr. Unsworth's shop. He was remanded in order that his 'antecedents might be obtained. A WIDNES COMPANY FINED FOR UNJUST SCALES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. J. C. Gamble, The Liverpool Silver and Copper Company, Limited, Ditton-road, were charged with having in their possession for use of trade, a pair of scales which were 15 ounces out of balance against the purchaser. Last week the manager of the works, Mr. Giblings, was summoned for the offence, but Mr. Husband contended that the Company should be summoned, and the case was therefore dismissed.—ln- spector Kilpatrick repeated his evidence, and Mr. Hus- band said there was no intention to defraud, as the weigher had attempted to make the scale correct. Cop- per was £47 a ton,and the scales in that condition would mean a gain of one halfpenny a ton.—The Bench im- posed a fine of £2 and costs. J. & W. LIBERAL CANDI D ATE FOR WARRINGTON.

Mr. Arthur Houston was horn in the city of. Dublin, on the 10th of August. 1833, and is the youngest son of the late Timothy Turner Houston, a Dublin trader. Ile is of Scotch extraction by his father's side, and a descendant, through his mother, of the old Irish family of Maguire, the clan to whom, before the days of " Settlements" and other forms of legalised confiscation, the county of Fermanagh belonged. From the school kept by Dr. Stackpoole, ' in Kingstown, where Lecky, the historian, was then a pupil, lie entered the University of Dublin, which strange to say, though it will this year celebrate the bi-centenary of its foundation, still contains but one College—" The College of the Holy and Un- divided Trinity of Queen Elizabeth, near Dublin," as the charter of foundation styles it. During his undergraduate course, Mr. Houston won a number of high distinctions in various sub- jects, and he took his degree of Bachelor of Arts. in 1857, obtaining, at the degree examination, Senior Moderatorship in History. Political Science, and English Literature. He subsequently pro- ceeded to the degrees of Master of Arts, and Doctor of Laws, and was appointed Whately Professor of Political Economy in 1861. He was called to the Irish bar in 1862, and filled for a time, las Deputy Professor, the chair of Feudal and English Law in the University. He was made a Queen's Council in 1882, and has at all times since he joined the legal profession enjoyed a large and varied practice. Ile has been counsel in some sensational cases, including the Maryborough trials, arising out of the death of District Inspector Martin, and the action for libel brought by Mr. Henry Campbell, M.P., the late Mr. Parnell's secretary, against Alder- man Hooper and others. Dr. Houston is married to a daughter of the late Henry Banks, M.D. He has been engaged in several public movements in his time, among others in the effort to establish Co- operative Societies in Ireland, and the agitation, started by the late Isaac Butt, in favour of an amnesty for the political prisoners convicted of participation in the Fenian rising. He is a Liberal of a robust type, and has taken an active part in promoting the cause of Home Rule, which he has advocated on many English platforms, as well as in Ireland at the meetings of the lush Protestant Home Rule association. His published writings include treatises upon the Inclussrial Disabilities of Women, the Constitution of Joint Stock Companies, I Indian Law, and other subjects.
DR. HOUSTON, Q.C., TUE

div.head: MAIL CART AND ITS HORSES.
div.p: THE MAIL CART AND ITS HORSES.

On Tuesday at Prescot Petty Sessions, Charles Burke, of Hollins Green, near Warrington, was summoned for allowing two horses to be worked in an unfit condition. Inspector Greatrex stated that about two o'clock on the morning of the Bth Dec- ember he examined the three horses of the Liver- pool and Manchester mail cart on their stoppage at Prescot. Two of the animals were found to be suffering from old sores, and were altogether unfit for the journey. Defendant was fined .Eland costs. J. & W. DITTTON'S ANNUAL WINTER SALE is now on. Sankey-st.--,Advt. GAS EXPLOSION AT ST. HELENS.

An alarming occurrence took place at 79, Argyle- St., the residence of a senior partner in the firm of Perkins Brothers, drapers, Bridge-st., on Monday afternoon. Mr. Perkins detected a smell of gas in the sitting-room. He threw open the window and door, and a short time afterwards re-entered with a light, and an explosion took place. A portion of the ceiling was blown down, and the flames set tire to the curtains at the window. Considerable damage was done to the furniture. Mr. Perkins fortunately escaped without personal injury, but suffered severely from shock. J. dc W. D'UTTON'S ANNUAL WINTER SALE is now on. Sankey-et.—.Advt.

div.head: DEATH FROM BLOOD POISONING AT WIDNES
div.p: DEATH FROM BLOOD POISONING AT WIDNES

Au inquest was held at Widnes Police Court on Tuesday, by Mr. W, T. Husband, the deputy coroner, touching the death of Mary Wilkinson aged 30 years, of 29 Moor-lane, A fortnight ago she was cleaning the fanlight when the bn upon which she was standing, slipped off the chair on which it was placed, and she tell into the street. Her right leg was injured in the same place where she had hurt it two years ago, and, blood poisoning setting in, she died on New Year's night. Dr. IHutchinson had attended the deceased. A verdict of "Accidental Death" was recorded.

div.head: EXTENSION OF W[DNES FREE LIBRA.RY,
div.p: EXTENSION OF W[DNES FREE LIBRA.RY,

DEFICIENT. A special meeting of Widnes Free Public Library Committee was held last evening, for the purpose of considering the provision of a boys' reading-room. Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.F., presided and there were present Messrs. P. .1. Brookes, S. Sadler, W. Sadler, Craik (clerk), J. Sinclair (surveyor), and Miss Proc- tor (Librarian).—The Surveyor had drawn a plan for the addition to the present readingroom of a room capable of accommodating about 100 boys at a cost of £lOO. It was explained that the room was very; necessary as the boys crowded out the men.—The Chairman said the Local Board had de- clined to make this provision because it was ex- pected that the town would be immediately incorl porated,and that the Town Hall would be completed which would involve an extension of the Library premises. The town was not now likely to be incorporated before next November, and he thought it would be well to ask the Local Board to re-consider their decision, as the room was urgently needed.—Mr. Sadler said the Local Board objected to spending .£lOO on a temporary room, and asked if it could be shown that the building could be utilized by some other department at a future time.—The surveyor said this could be done. The present plans for the Town Hall would have to be altered. In the first place, the Boardroom would be too small for a Council Chamber, because the Council would consist of 36 members instead of 15 members. It was then?decided,on the motion of Mr.Brookes, seconded by Mr. W. Sadler, to ask the Local Board to re-con- sider their decision.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

Upon the reading of the minutes of the last meet- ing. Dr. McDougall said £l6O had been advanced by the Commissioners for the purchase of apparatus, and he wished to know first, if the money had been profitably spent ; secondly, whether the Board had undertaken the care of the apparatus; thirdly, whether they were to be held responsible for any damage done to the articles during the period they were in the custody of the Board; and fourthly, whether any steps had been taken or would be taken to relieve the Board of the responsibility.— The Chairman said Dr. McDougall was chairman of the Science and Art Committee,and this was within the province of that Committee.—Dr. McDougall re- plied that it was entirely outside that Committee,to whom the communications were not addressed and who had not the custody of the apparatus.—The Clerk said the apparatus would be in the custody of the Board distinct from any committee.—Dr. McDougall said it seemed to him that the School Board was merely the stepping-stone for the pur- chase of these articles and that they would be re- lieved of the responsibility when the Technical ' Institute was established.—The Chairman said it was for the Science and Art Committee to say whether the money had been profitably spent. div.head: COLLISION ON TITE RAILWAY NEAR WIDNES.
div.p: COLLISION ON TITE RAILWAY NEAR WIDNES.

A serious collision between two goods trains took place on the Cheshire Lines Railway at CuerElley Junction on Thursday morning. About half-past four two trains were approaching the junction,one from Widnes and another from Liverpool and the driver of the latter, seeing the signal against him applied his brake, but probably because of the accummulation of snow on the metals, the brake did not act, and the engine dashed into the middle of the Widnes train. Three wagons were smashed to mate-11,700d and many others were thrown off the line, and both lines were entirely blocked. Happily no one was injured. As soon as pos- sible two break down gangs were on the scene, but it was not until 12 noon that the debris was cleared away, and the traffic resumed its ordinary course. During this time, however, the passenger traffic had suffered little delay. District Inspector Denning had made ample arrangements for conveying passengers to and from Liverpool and Manchester by special trains from the scene of the accident,and this arrangement worked very will.

div.head: FATAL RESULT OF A DRUNKEN SPREE AT RUNCORN. WALKING INTO THE MERSEY.
div.p: FATAL RESULT OF A DRUNKEN SPREE AT RUNCORN. WALKING INTO THE MERSEY.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner for the honor and fee of Halton, on Tuesday held an inquest at Run- corn Cemetery office,on the body of Peter Phelp,aged 20 years, of Parr, Cornwall, and a cook and seaman on board the schooner Kate and Annie, of Fowey, Corn- wall, who was found drowned in the Mersey, at the en- trance to Runcorn Docks,on Sunday.—Joshua Bennett,a sailor, said he and the deceased were drinking together in Runcorn on Saturday night, and after closing time they were returning to the ship toeether. He (witness) was drunk and the deceased was worse. At the docks they both fell down, and when he (witness) got on his feet again he saw the deceased walking some distance ahead. He shouted to him, but he took no heed, and in a few moments he was out of sight. He went on board the ship, but came on shore again in order to try to find the deceased, but he could not see him anywhere. He did not know what time it would be. —The Coroner: Were you very drunk ? Witness : I was not senseless. I knew where the vessel was lying alone the Quay, and I had sense enough to get on board the vessel.—Royle Garnett, a pierhead man, deposed that about midnight on Saturday the deceased came into the room on the pierhead where the ropes are kept. He was very drunk,and fell asleep. About two o'clock he awoke,and appeared much better. He walked straight and appeared capable of reaching his vessel, otherwise witness would have taken him there, as he had sailors on many occasions. From the position in ' which the body was found it would seem that deceased had walked off the end of the pier.—Thomas Bostock, a mariner from Winsford, deposed to recoverieg the body. —Mr. Ford, the Cemetery keeper, said there were no marks of violence on the body.—The Coroner said he at first thought, when he received the police report, that it was a case of desertion by the first witness, but he was happy now to think that it was not so. Sailors were a most affectionate class of people and looked- well after on another more than other classes.—The jury returned a Verdict of" Found Drowned."

div.head: FOOTBALL
div.p: FOOTBALL

WIDNES A T. ST. HELENS A.—Played at Widnes on Saturday, and the home won by two tries to nil. reterS and Jackson were the scorers. ST. HELENS Y. WIDNES (A THAtts.)—ThiS inatch was Played on Saturday at Widnes, in wretched weather. Final result ::-Widnes A four points, St. Helena A nil.

RUNCORN RECREATION V. Witsisat. This match should have been played at Runcorn on Saturday after- noon, but the Wirral team never put in an appearance, much to the regret of the home team, who had antici- pated having a good game. ST. HELENS V. RIINCORN.—PIayed at St. Helens on New Year's Day, the home team being short of Cross ; and Runcorn were without Crompton,Riley, Shaw, Williams, and Hughes. Faulknerkicked off, St. Helens rushing the ball back, and scoring a minor. St. Helens kept up the pressure, Doherty having a free kick, which Houghton returned grandly. After some severe scrimmaging Abrams put in. a strong run and passed to Davies, who ran in grandly. Even play followed, when Little gave the hall to Doherty, and this player scored for St. Helens. Rennie restarted after half-time, and, following well up, a scrimmage was formed on the Runcorn line, and they were for a time busily occupied in defending. Brown- bill afterwards scored for St. Helens. Runcorn after- wards had the best of matters. Final result—St. Helens, 4 points ; Runcorn, 2 points. ST. HELENS V. WIDNES.—These rival teams met at St. Helens, on Saturday afternoon, before 3,000 spectators. Additional interest centred in the encounter by reason of the fact that on the previous day St. Helens had de- feated Runcorn. The home team won the toss, and played wish a strong wind in their favour during the first half. The homesters gradually pressed the Widnes men on their line, and after a series of scrimmages near the posts Johnson met the ball and kicked it over the bar, amid loud cheers, thus scoring what proved to be the only goal of the match. Before half time the Widnes forwards got to the opposite end, but were unable to break through the home defence. In the second half Widnes played hard, and, favoured with the breeze, had much the best of the game. St. Helens defended well, however, and defeated the efforts of their opponents. The play was exciting towards the close, but St. Helens had the upper hand, and won by 4 points to nil.
RUNCORN v.- SALE.

• This match was played at Sl.e,Wl—S—a.turday. Consider- able interest was taken in the meeting, and, although the prospects of Sale lowering the Runcorn c)lours were indeed remote, a good number assembled in the hope of seeing the locals give their renowned rivals a good game. In this they were disappointed, for the Runcorn men, passing and dribbling with ease and precision, completely routed the Sale defence. Winning the toss. Drinkwater was deputed to kick off for Sale. The opening items were anything but favourable for the homesters, for a sharp bout of passing by Abram, Crompton and Davies was followed by Houghton dropping a fine goal. this was only the forerunner of a capital exhibition between Croinpori and Abrams, which realized a try by Pendlebury. Davies followed next, and whilst the attack was maintained Pendlebury notched his second try, Faulkner landing a goal. Rain marred the game to some extent, but it did not prevent the Cheshire champions from acting the pant of aggressors, and Davies, as the result of some brilliant passiu,,, notched another try, which Crompton converted. The second half was a repetition of the first portion, and beyond Drinkwater, Sale displayed but poor form. Riley was amongst the scorers in the second half, and a one-sided game concluded as follows :—Runcorn, 5-4-0 ; Sale 0-0-0.

A YOUNG DRFRAUDER.—On Tuesday. at Prescat Petty Sessions, John Eden, a lad, was charged with obtaining by false pretences a sixpence, a loaf of bread, and a box of starch from Mrs. Ann Ledward, a Prescot shopkeeper. Prisoner alleged that a neighbour had sent him for the articles. He was ordered to be given six strokes with a birch rod.

div.head: DR. HOUSTON AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: DR. HOUSTON AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

On Thursday evening, Dr. Houston, accompanied by Mr. W. Pierpoint and Councillor H. Roberts,paid a visit to the Liberal Club, and was introduced to many of the members who were present in different parts of the build- ing. At a social gathering of workers of Orford Ward, Mr. W. Roberts, who presided, proposed the health of the candidate, and this tout was cordially honoured. Cheers were also given for Mrs. Houston, Dr. Houston, who was present at the tine, speaking on behalf of his wife and himself, returned his hearty thanks for the way in which the toast had been proposed and received. The Chairman had referred to the way in which he was re- ceived the previous night, and he must say that of all welcomes, a Warrington welcome "takes the cake." (Applause and laughter.) He was not only greatly sur- prised but he was astonished that as a stranger could be received in the manner in which he was received the , previous night. It had given him great courage in what they must all admit would boa very stirring fight. There appeared to be no doubt, that an opportunity had pre- sented itself for wresting the borough from the hands of the Tories as had not been enjoyed for many a long day, and now it would be his duty,and, of course, their duty, and the duty of every member of the Liberal party in Warrington to see that most was made of the opportunity. (Hear, hear and applause.) From what he had heard and seen,that success was not only possible but probable, if they worked as they ought to do. That was just one of the constituencies in which the election might be ' turned by a very small number, and therefore it became the imperative duty of every person who had the well- being of the Liberal party at heart to leave no stone unturned to secure even a single vote. (Hear, hear.) They, of course, did not know when the general election might be sprung upon them, but they must exert them- selves just as though the election was coming next week or the week after next: They were fighting for a good cause, and he thought that, if they put their shoulders to the wheel and acquitted themselves like men that good cause would triumph at the next election. (Loud ap- plause.)
Dr. Houston afterwards left Warrington to take the night boat to Dublin. During his stay in the town, he was the guest of Mr. John Rylands, J.P., president of the Liberal Association.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Mall, on Thursday. Mr. H. J. Once presided and there were present Messrs. W. Fisher, J. Pritchard, W. Timmins, D. Bisbrown, F. Wiscvall, H. Coward, R. Abel, P. Smith, H. White, J. W. Lightburn, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (sec.), W. Barker (surveyor), and Dr. McDougall (medical officer).

div.head: EPIDEMIC OF-MEASLES.
div.p: EPIDEMIC OF-MEASLES.

-----.— The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amounts to 55. Of these deaths one was an inquest case and of the remaining 54, 22 were due to measles, 5 to bronchitis, 2to cancer, 2 to heart disease, 1 to child- birth, 2 to puerperal fever, 2 to typhoid fever, 2 to mesenteric disease, 3 to senile decay, 4 to convulsions, and one each to pleurisy, peritonitis, croup, defective nutrition, defective development, pneumonia, plithisis, and kidney diseases. The 55 deaths showed an average death-rate of 33 per 1,000 of the estimlted population, and, exclusive of the inquest case, of 32.4. The Autho- rity would observe that the large death-rate was due to the prevalence of measles during the past month and the inclement weather. He had reason to believe that the somewhat severe epidemic of measles that had been pre- vailing for some time was now on the decline.

div.head: lUNCORN HILL.
div.p: lUNCORN HILL.

On the reeommendation of the Highways Committee it was resolved that notice be served on the Marquis of Cholmondeley to make good the fence at the Quarry on Runcorn Hill, at certain places to be indicated by the surveyor.

div.head: CANAL BOATS ACTS.
div.p: CANAL BOATS ACTS.

The Canal Boats Committee submitted the annual re- port to the Local Government Board as to the execution of the Canal Boats Acts. It stated that 19 boats had been registered during the year, making a total of 922 registered at Runcorn. There had been 23 contraven- tions of the Acts and regulations reported to the commit- tee, and the committee were satisfied that these contra- ventions had been remedied. 300 inspections of boats had I been made during the year, and the inspector found 449 men, 113 women,and 133 children of 14 years of age and under, on board the boats inspected. With regard to the education of the children, the inspector reported that many of the parents preferred to pay the fines for non- attendance of their children at school rather than lose their labour. There had again been a diminution in the number of women on board, but there was no increase in the number of children. THE TEHICULAR BRIDGE ACrcOSS THE MERSEY The Mersey Bridge Committee recommended that the seal of the Board be affixed to a joint memorial by the Local Board for the town of Widnes and the Improve- ment Commissioners for the town of Runcorn to the respective County Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire urging their immediate consideration of the question of the construction of a bridge over the River Mersey con- necting the two counties at Runcorn and that Major Ilazlehurst and Mr. P. Speakman, who are the repre- sentatives of the town of Runcorn in the Cheshire County Council be requested to present such memoria 1 to their Council. That copies of the Memorial be sent to the neighbouring authorities and that they be asked to further the object.—Mr. Wiswall moved the confirm- ation of the minutes.—Mr. Liglithurn seconded the m)tion.—The motion Was carried unanimously.
- DEEP /KICKS roe RUNCORN. Mr. Lightburn asked the Secretary whether he had received any communication from the Ship Canal Co:n-

pans' with respect to the deputation that it was arranged I should wait upon them with reference to deep docks at Runcorn,—The Secretary replied in the negative.—Mr. Lightburn said he wished it to be well known that the Commissioners had been waiting for the last two months for an appointment in this year, and as the new year had now commenced he suggested that the Secretary should write and point out the importance of the subject and press for an immediate appointment. Technical Schools and a bridge across the Mersey were most important, but of supreme importance was the question of deep docks. (Hear, hear.) It was no use having technical schoels—and no one felt more anxious that V-ey should be developed than he was—unless we had a population to attend the schools.—Mr. Fisher seconded Mr. Lightburn's suggestion,and the Secretary was unani- mously instructed to write accordingly.

THE EASTBOURNII SALVATION ARMY RIOTS. The Secretary read a long letter from the Mayor of , Eastoourne with regard t® a clause in their Improve- ment Act, which provided that no procession should take I place on Snnday in the borough accompanied by instru- men.al music. This section was obtained •five years before the Salvation Army made their appearance in Eastbourne, and the inhabitants were determined to retain the section and enforce its provisions. The Mayor wished several questions he forwarded to be answered, ' the principal one asking if the Board approved of the sec- tion and if they would support a bill for making it appli- cable to every Corporation and local Authority.—Mr. Lightburn said he did not think the letter was worth , wasting time over.—Mr. Smith moved that it be ack- nowledged and be laid on the table.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion.—Mr. Bisbrown moved an amend- ment strongly condemning the action of the Eastbourne Corporation in respect to their interference with the Salvation Army services, and said that there would be legislation on this subject in the near future.—Tho Chairman said Mr. Bisbrown was off the fact in saying that the Mayor of Eastbourne was desirous of attempting to interfere with freedom of speech or freedom of procession. The bye-law referred to bands, horns, and trumpets causing noise and annoyance. He should be the last one to say a word about the Salvation Army or any other institution that might be for the , benefit of the nation; at the same time it was advisable I that every law-abiding citizen should abide by the law, and if the Salvation Army in our midst attempted to do anything which was in opposition to a byelaw he should say they were not acting strictly in accordance with what they professed. He thought in the present case there was a little sympathy to be expressed for both sides.—Mr. Lightburn said allowing the letter to lie on the table would express the feelings of the Board.—Mr. Wiswall supported the motion. There was a good deal to be said on both sides and their wisest course would be to let the letter lie on the table—Mr. Pritchard supported the motion because it wouid be best for the Board to remain neutral in the matter.—The motion was carried, only Mr. Bisbrown voting against.

TRADES UNIONS AND CONTRACTS. The Secretary said he had received the following let- ter from Mr. A. G. Lowery, secretary to the Widnes and District Trades Council. "At the last monthly meeting of the Coun.iil the following resolution was un- animously adopted :—That this Council impressed with the evils disclosed in the sweating system respectfully request the local authorities to insert in all their con- tracts provisions against subletting any of their con- tracts that can be performed by the contractor himself. Also that one contract be given to any firm or firms that do not conform to the recognised customs and hours of labour laid down by the Trade Unions in the district. Also that no contract for labour only be recog- nised as valid.—Mr. Lig,htburn said that letter involved a very great question.—The Chairman said he thought the case would be met if the Secretary acknowledged I reciept of the letter. - -------

_ SCIENCE AND ART CLASSEC—FIIRTHER DEVELOPMENT. Writing as secretary to the Science and Art Commit- tee, Mr. G. MOBS said :—"Referring to your letter of the 7th August, 1891, stating that your Board would make good any deficiency in connection with the above classes during the current session to the extent of £75, I'beg to inform you that the classes now established will absorb that amount, and perhaps £5 or £lO more. My committee are also about to inaugurate classes for cooking and dressmaking, which will further increase the deficit ; also they are desirous that I should have some remuneration for my services as organising secre- tary. lam therefore directed to ask your Board to be good enough to increase the aforesaid limit to the sum of £l5O. This will leave a little margin for any further work that may be undertaken, and whatever balance is left will, of course, be returnable to your Board."—The communication was referred to the Legal Committee, it being understood that there would be no objection to granting a reasonable amount. THE CONDITION OF HIGH-ST.. .

Mr. Smith proposed that the Surveyor be instructed to put the flags in repair that he had pulled up or caused to be pulled up in High-st. It was a disgrace to the Sur- veyor and to the town that such a state of things should exist. He was told that there had been a watchman there for a fortnight when no work was going on.—The Surveyor : Quite untrue.—After some discussion the Chairman thought the Surveyor had done his best under the eircumstances.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Dr. Steele. TEDSPORARY Atrrnonivv. Mrs. Green was granted temporary authority to sell at the Royal Oak Inn, under the license lately held by her husband, Mr. Wm. Green, deceased. YOUNG GAMBLERS.—Wm. Jones, Samuel Green, John Feeney, Alfred Bothwell, George Woodfine, and Francis Collins, all boys under 15 years, were charged with hiv- ing on Christmas night, in Cooper-st., played with cards, at the game of banker. The eefendant pleaded guilty, but said they were not playing for money be- cause they had none. P.C.'s Booth and Proctor said they did not see money, but they heard it. They went to the place in consequence of complaints. The boys were playing by the light of a street lamp. The magis- trates dismissed the case on payment of costs, or in de- fault seven days' impriienment.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAT.—Before Mr. H. W. Deacon and Mr. J. Birettall.
DRUNKENNESS—For this offence fines of ss. and costs were imposed upon Thos. McDermot, Wm. Peers, Eliza- beth Peel, and Geo. Loundes.

ASSAULT ON THE POLlCE.—Daniel King, of no fixed abode, was charged with being drunk and disorderly,and with assaulting P.C. Crane. When arrested on the first charge the prisoner acted very violently and kicked the constable on the legs. Re also attempted to bite hi m.— A fine of ss. and costs was imposed for the first offence and 10s. and costs for the second offence.

A LUNATIC. —7\llrtin Quinn, Warrington-road, was charged with being a wandering lunatic.—P.C. Reid stated that Quinn came running to him about five o'clock on Monday morning in Lugsdale-road and shouted that two men were running after him with axes to kill him. He brought him to the police station.—The Bench sent him to the Workhouse for a fortnight in order that he might have the attention of a medical man.

div.head: F RODSLIA.M.
div.p: F RODSLIA.M.

ACCIDENT TO A CARTER.—A very serious accident occur- red at Sutton, on Saturday morning, to a carter named John Pemberton. who was conveying a load of furniture to Frodsham Bridge. Some how or other, Pemberton Slipped on the ground, and one of the cart wheels pas.sed over him, fracturing his collar bone, crushing his arm, besides inflicting some internal injuries. PIZAS&NT EVENINGS.—There is still a marked interest shown by t', large attendances at the Saturday evening concerts 'l.in the schoolroom, Chapel-lane. The pro- gramme ot Saturday was much enjoyed, consisting of pianoforte solos by Miss Bessie Lewis, cornet and violin duets by Mr. and Miss Guest, of Flelsby ; Mr. Guest also rendered the cornet solos, " The better land "and "The Lost Chord." Recitation and reading by Miss N. Simcock. Songs by Miss Agnes Wrench and Mr. John Hancock.
THE FIRST WARtINGTON STARR- BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.

The fifth annual meeting of this Society. vvas held in Legh-st. Schoolroom on Thursday evening. Mr. John Walker presided, and there was a fair attend- ance of members. The Secretary (Mr. J. Titchett) read the annual report as follows:—" The subscrip- tions for the year amount to £1,567 17s. 4d. Entrance fees, transfer of appropriations, fines, and bank interest, &c.£7l Is. 3d.; repayments of ap- propriations and solicitor's fees .£505 163. ; snaking a total income of .C 2,144 14s. 7d.; and leaving the balance of profit in favour of the Society .£ll5 7s. Sd. Thirty-five appropriations have now been made since the Society was formed, and the next will be made at the Annual meeting, Thursday, January 7th. The total amount now advanced to the members, free of interest is £7,580, and the re- payments .C 1,199 78.. leaving the sum of £6,389 13s. due to the Society. The retiring directors are Messrs. Brown, Crampton, Hickman, and Sumner, and thd offer themselves for re-election. The auditors, lessrs. Milliard and Pearson, also retire, and being eligible offer themselves for re-election." The report was unanimously adopted. Messrs. Brown, Hickman, Denham and CritchleLiTaerrg elected directors, and Messrs. Pearson and were re-elected auditors. A vote of thanks was accorded the Chairman. Mr. I ' lickmar presided over a subsequent appropriation meeting. The bal- lot resulted in the drawing of 449 which entitled Mr. T. Peet, 9, Grant-st., Earlestown, to £2OO free of interest for 124 years.
