div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
_ • "BrAN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."_

Since Mr. Deacon became the accepted candidaZe of the Liberal party in the Widnes Division he has greatly improved in one respect. Although for some years he has taken an active part in public affairs in Widnes, he was seldom seen or heard on a platform, and his style as a speaker was more con- versational than oratorical. The experience he has recently had in addressing meetings in various parts of the Division, has been of great benefit to him, and he has greatly improved in his speaking. ith appropriate gesture and expression he now delivers himself of short crisp sentences that are full of meaning in a manner that declares that he is convinced of what he advocates and which conse- quently has a convincing effect upon his auditory. This will be all to his advantage when the battle i commences n earnest, as there are votes to be won at public meetings by good arguments put in a convincing manner.

-- One of the questions now being asked by some Church people in Runcorn, is why the clergy went round begging subscriptions for the tea party. Ac- cording to the published figures, the tea party has not only paid its way but left a surplus. Subscrip- tions appear to have been given amounting to £l6 78., and the tea party profit of 17s. 40., swells I this to £l7B. 4s. 40. Is this sum going like many lothers to aid the Curate's Stipend Account ?

The Rev. C. F. Montgomery, 8.A., the latest addi- tion to the clergy staff, at Runcorn Parish Church, was educated at Glenalmond School at Pembroke College, Cambridge. He also studied a year at Leeds Clergy School and was ordained Deacon by the Bis- hop in Chester Cathedral on the fourth Sunday in Advent. Mr. Montgomery will be more particularly attached to the Parish Church, and will visit in the district lying between Bridgewater-st.,and the river including Waterloo-road and Duke's Field.

Speaking of the above one cannot help calling to mind the number of curates the present vicar has. It is absolutely necessary that there should be so many? The natural inquiry is what is the vicar himself doing? It may be that it takes all his time tc direct his curates in their duties, but perhaps he is qualifying for the office of Bishop.

It is the wonder of many tow it is that that the vicar seems to consider he has the oversight of the whole of Runcorn, and does not appear to count in the reckoning all those who are taking a share of the work. The other clergy, say of Trinity and the various ministers of the gospel, are surely doing something to win Runcorn from the error of its way into the paths of sobriety and holiness and deserve recognition. It would be well if there was a little more unity and harmony in seeking to attain these ends.

When the assisted Education Act was passed, the Education Department sent out a ciicular urging that in schools where advantage was taken of the Act for abolishing or reducing the fees,banks should be formed where the children might save the pence no longer required as school fees. In connection with Runcorn Parish Schools, a scholars bank is to be opened on Monday next in connection With the Post Office Savings Bank, and it is to be hoped there , will be many young depositors.

The Rev. Hudson Shaw, M.A., fellow of Balliol College, Oxford, two years ago, inaugurated the University Extension Movement in Runcorn, by a series of lectures on Social Reformers. A course of ! six lectures on Florence will be commenced on Monday evening, and the fee is as low as circum- stances will allow, and within the reach of work-
_ __— people. The Committee have been fortunate in again securing Mr. Hudson Shaw as lecturer. His graphic descriptions will be aided by numerous limelight views.

I am happy to be in a position to state that Mr. Bowdon, C' .E. of Manchester, has prepared two sketch plans of the proposed Technical Institute in Waterloo-road, and the Committee have adopted one which shows a building three stories high (in- cluding the basement), and of some architectural pretentions, although as might be expected, beauty has had to give way to utility.

It has been frequently said that there is a special providence watching over drunken men, because, I presume, of the manifold dangers they so marvel- lously escape in their wanderings when bereft of proper locomotion and their minds a perfect blank. All are not so fortunate and Peter Phelp a young sailor,in a search tor his vessel at the Dock,on Satur- day night, walked of the end of the pier, and was picked up next day a stiffened corpse. A companion also drunk, but not" senseless," reached his vessel more by good luck than by good management, and is left to repent and to amend his ways.

A meeting of the Provincial Grand Lodge of Cheshire, was held at Knutsford, on Thursday, when addresses of congratulation, were sent to the Prince of Wale's. and the Duke of Clarence. The brethren present from this district, were T. H. Annett,P.M. Provincial Treasurer; W. Mellor, P.M, P.P.G.J.D. ;C. Phillips, S.W.; W. Hankinson, S.D. Colonel Ashton P.M., (Cholmondeley Lodge) and H. C. Heywood, P.P.G., standard bearer (Cholmon- deley Lodge). I hear from a good source that up to date there has been raised in the province of Chester, the sum of .£l,OOO towards the aged Free- masons' and widows of Freemasons' Benevolent Fund, in celebration of the jubilee of that charitable branch of the Craft. This is exclusive of a donation of fifty guineas from Lord Egerton. tile Right Worshipful Provincial Grand Master. Freemasonry is evidently a living and fruitful force in Cheshire.

In connection-Wiiii-The -Wesleyan Mutual Im- provement Association an essay entitled "Chris- tian Symbols," was read by Mr. J. Garnett of Chester, on Wednesday evening. There was a moderate attendance.

div.head: WARRINGTON _RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON _RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

Mr. W. over the meeting of this Authority,vvhich was held at tne Workhouse yester- day. The Clerk (Mr.S.Slitton) reported that several townships were in arrears with their calls, and he was instructed to write threatening proceedings if the calls were not immediately paid. Replies were read from different sanitory authorities upon the subject of gas lighting and the manner in which the expenses were charged, after which Mr. W. Houghton proposed his motion to rescind the re- solution passed in September last, in order to make lighting a special charge upon each township, in- stead of a general charge upon the whole district. —Mr. Heaton moved, and Mr. Dobson seconded, an amendment that the resolution remain unaltered. Five voted for the amendment and five against, and as the Chairman gave his casting vote in favour of the amendment it was carried.—A petition was read from some inhabitants of Padgate,to the effect that public gas lighting was not needed in the township, but the Clerk pointed out that the lighting arrange- ments had been agreed to at a meeting of rate- payers at which he was present, and also by the Sanitary Authority on two occasion. No action was taken on the petition. The rest of the business was of a formal character. HEALTH AND WEATHER OP WARRINGTON. For week ending Saturday, 2nd Jan., 1892, which was the Ist of the current year, the following births and deaths were , registered :—Births: War- rington, 41; Latchford, 5; total 46. Deaths: War- rington, 24; Latchford, 3; total 27. The excess of births ovtr deaths was 19. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 26.5 per 1,000 against 2791, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 32 the corresponding week of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 3'o per 1,000, against 417, the average rate of the four previous weeks, aid against nil the corresponding week of 1891. The ages of mortality, were- 0 to 1, 7 ; 1 to 5,4; 5 to 15,3; 15 to 25, 0 ; 25 to 60, 9; 60 upwards, 4; total 27. The deaths included-2 from scarlet fever, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from measles, 1 from Addison's disease, 1 1 from parturition, 1 from kidney disease, 1 from heart disease, 1 from brain disease, 12 from lung , disease, 2 from liver disease. The following eases of infectious disease have been reported during the week :—Typhoid fever 1 case, diphtheria 3 3 cases, scarlatina 11 eases. Meteorology—The mean t„ temperature was 41.2 Fah., and therefore 13.1 deg- I higher than the preceding week. The maximum temverature 51 F., was recorded on the 29th ult., and the minimum temperature 32 F., on the 27th ult. The rainfall measured 110 inches. The general direction of the wind was S.W., the reading of the Anemometer denoting 1,230 miles.—Jourt 11, GoutiaLL, Medical Officer of Health,

div.head: TilE REPRESENTATION OF
div.p: TilE REPRESENTATION OF
WARRINGTON.
ELECTION OF A LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

„ADDRESS BY DR. HOUSTON, Q.C. On Wednesday evening a crowded and enthusiastic meeting of the Liberal 300 of Warrington was held at the Liberal Club for the purpose of hearing an address by Dr. Houston. Q.C., of Dublin, and after- wards considering the advisability of inviting that gentleman to become the Liberal candidate for War- rington. Mr. J. Rylands, IP., the president of the Liberal Association, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Mr. W. Pierpoint, Councillor F. A. Roberts, Dr. Gornall, J.P., Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., Councillors H. Roberts, G. Plumpton, A. Browne, and S. J. Beaman, Rev. J. W. Varley ; Messrs. T. Morris, F. Longdin, W. Roberts, J. Walker, Kiernan, S. Kenyon, T. Birchall, J. Albinson, D. Tinnion, J. Mounfield, C. J. Holmes, S. Dunbobbin., THB CHAIRMAN'S AIM:MISS.

The CFIAIRMIN. who was received with much ap- plause, after thanking the audience for their recep- tion of him, said it took him hack a good many years when he used to enter pretty considerably in- to the election fight in that borough. He could a tale unfold—(laughter)—but .he thought it was hardly the occasion for it. He believed they were there that night for the especial purpose of form- ing the acquaintance of Dr. Houston. He for one was very pleased to have the opportunity of doing so. He unfortunately never met the doctor before, but the impression he had formed of him from what he had learnt from certain sources was of a very favourable character, and he believed from what a mutual friend had told him that they would also be favourably impressed. One word about the election, for there would certainly be an election before long. He was not a prophet. He sometimes tried to prophesy, but it was generally in consequence of having considerable experience in the past in reference to the subject about which he prophesied. Now, he was bound to say that he had not sufficient knowledge how to prophesy with regard to .the result of the coming election. The fact was the fortunes of Warrington had been very -variable, and there Was no telling what might hap- pen. He could only say this that it appeared to him that at the present time the Libcrals had a better prospect than they had had for several years. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt about it, that there had been very important changes in the borough during the last few years. There was an in- crease of the population,and a change in the indivi- duals of the populatioA. Some gentlemen present might know very much about it, and might be able to encourage Dr. Houston—and encourage him he hoped they would—but anyhow what they had to do was to make a good fight. The melancholy part of the subject was this,that they had got in Warrington a very la„re number of public-houses; and public- ans, almost to a man, he believed were Tories. That was a very difficult nut to crack. Formerly he knew, in the days before the ballot they were so; and he had reason to suspect that there had been some- , thing going on at recent elections which would not bear daylight. Now; what their business was, Was to try to counteract the influence of this pub- licans. He hoped some of them would be able to give encouragement to Dr. Ho, iston ; at any rate he was quite sure from the meeting he saw that night, there would be some very good workers,who would deserve success if they did not get it. (Applause.) The Chairman then called upon Dr. Houston to address the meeting. DR. 110IISPON'5 Dr. HOUSTON, who was greeted with loud applause, said: Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, I assure you that I am not going thrcugh any mere idle form when I tell you that I feel the greatest pride and the greatest satis- faction in being afforded an opportunity of addressing this assembly of the representatives .of Liberal opinion in Warrington, and whatever may be the result of your , deliberations to-night I shall never forget the kindly wel- come with which I have been received and the many friends it has been my privilege to make in connection with the invitation that was conveyed to me to come and lay my views beton. you. Now, this is a very im- portant business in which we are engaged to-night, important for you and important for me. The selection of a candidate upon any occasion is a matter of moment to the constituents, but the issues which are involved in the next general election are of so momentous a charac- ter that it invests this occasion and this meeting with an importance which such meetings seldom possess. On the

RESULT OF TILE NEXT GENERAL ELECTION 1 will depend the liberties of one of the three kingdoms— (hear, hear)—and the happiness and the progress of all three kingdoms. (Hear, hear and applause.) Therefore it behoves the constituents to take every precaution to see that the man that they select to carry the Liberal flag in the next great electoral battle is a man upon whom they can rely—(hear, hear)—is a man who is in entire sympathy with the aims and the objects and the views of the great Liberal party, and is willing and able by vote and by voice to give effect to those views and those aims and those objects, if lie has the honour to be elected to represent them in Parliament. Now, I am here to-night to explain to you as briefly as I can what my opinions are, and I am happy to think you will find before I am done, from what I know of the stuff that the Liberals of Warrington are made of, that my views and theirs are in complete accord. (Hear, hear.) There are, of course, a large number of questions a'nd subjects that it will be unnecessary for me to touch upon at all. There are questions which have passed out of the region of discussion entirely. We Liberals of this generation have SUCCEEDED TO A GREAT HERITAGE of rights that have been won and principles that have been established by the Liberals of the past. (Hear, hear.) Personal freedom; freedom of speech , freedom of worship, freedom of the press, and freedom of trade —all these have been won far us by those who have carried the Liberal flag in titnes gone by, and our duty with regard to them is not so much to discuss them, or unnecessarily assert our duty with regard to them as to protect and preserve them for those who are to come after us. (Applause.) Sometimes we shall be called upon actively to exert ouselves. If you take the case, for instance, of
FREE TRADE.

although it has been an accepted principle in these coun- tries for many a longlrear,- strange to say we find that not only on the Continent of Europe, in the United States of America, but even in the self-governing colonies of this Empire; Free Trade is not recognised. We find it also assailed even in these countries under the insidious title of Fair Trade, and it would be our duty to see that that great principle of Free Trade is not undermined or sapped by any rash insidious suggestions such as are contained under the title Fair Trade. (Hear, hear and applause.) Again, although, happily,you are in the en- joyment of your full. liberties at. this side of the water, OUR LIBERTIES HAVE BEEN ASSAILED AND CURTAILED at the other side of the water. Trial by jury has been practically suspended in a large number of cases ; free- dom of speech, the freedom of the press, and the freedom of public meeting have been curtailed if not destroyed, and that shows you that although we have secured these great rights and established these great principles, or rather they have been secured and established for us, we must be watchful and ready and prepared to defend and sustain them as they may be attacked hereafter. (Applause.) But these were not the questions which you expect a candidate for this constituency to give you his opinions and views upon.:They are taken for granted. What you want to hear from me to-night, as I under- stand, are my views and my opinions upon what are THE QUESTIONS OF OUR OWN DAY and our own generation. (Hear, hear.) Now, what are those questions ? What are the questions that are occupying the time and the minds and the energies of the Liberal party ? Well,it is not easy for me to answer that inquiry, and for this reason. About 15 years ago, as I best recollect, a great organisation was established for the purpose of collecting and recording the opinions of Liberals throughout the country—l allude to the National Liberal Federation—and by means of that or- ganisation and by means of the annual meeting of the delegates held under its auspices, we are enabled year by year. not merely to observe the progress which Libe- ral opinions and Liberal principles have made in the past, but to ascertain what are the views which the Liberals of the country entertain upon the pressing questions of the day. I had the privilege and the ad- vantage of being present at the great meeting that was held last autumn in Newcastle, and there I heard the discussion upon the different questions that were pre- sented to the meeting for their consideration, and I had an opportunity of considering then and since the LIBERAL PROGRAMME

that was then promulgated. To place myself in a clear position with this meeting I state now that by that pro- gramme lam prepared to stand. (Applause.) Now, that programme deals with a great variety of subjects, SO great a variety indeed that the only criticism which is i being passed upon it is that it s too extensive, that is too wide, too far-reaching for the taste at least of our Opponents. (Applause and laughter.). And accordingly it has been criticised in that vein, and lam sorry to say that among the critics that have taken up. that attitude is a man who was at all events once a Liberal and who professes to be a Liberal still—Mr. Chamber- lain—(" Oh, oh "\—and he has gone the length of say- ing that because it, is a wide and far-reaching pro- gramme of policy therefore it is a dishonest programme.l dunk he must have been thinking of some of the tricks of his new pies. (sear, hear and lauohter.) It is not usual for Liberals to put out bogus programmes ; they are in the habit when they make promises of keeping them when they have the opoortunity to do so,and they gener- ally either fird or make the opportunity. (Hear, hear.) Now, as I said before, that programme is very wide and far-reaching and includes a greatyariety of subjects,and in discussing it, it is difficult to know where to begin,

and where to leave off, but I think that by a little group- 1 ing and classification, I shall be able briefly to review a considerable number of the questions suggested by that 1 programme. Of course I shall not be able to touch upon all questions contained in it, and I hope that it will not be taken that my omitting to do so, in any particalar case is an indication that Ido not consider the omitted question one of great importance, for they are all of great importance—(hear hear)—but time is short and art is long and we must only do our best with the space which necessarily must be placed at the disposal of a person in my position to-night. The first class of ques- tions, with which that programme deals is a group of what I may call Constitutional questions, and the first of these, indeed the first on the programme of the National Federation, is

HONE RULE!. (Applause.) Now, I propose to night to give the Irish question a holiday, or, if I may use the expression, a half-holiday, because I think if there be a question upon which you may safely trust me it is the Irish question. (Loud applause and laughter.) Speakers at Liberal meetings are no longer afraid that if they do not discuss Home Rule at inordinate length they would be told that Home Rule is as dead as Queen Anne. Since the New- castle meeting I have not observed that Mr. Chamberlain has made the slightest reference to that deceased potent- ate. (Laughter.) 4ortly, I put it in this way—l am a Liberal arid I am an irishman—(hear, hear)—and there- fore I am under a double obligation to fight for Home Rule. I will only make one observation on the Irish question and it is this—you may take it from me that the mass of the Irish people are absolutely faithful to the alliance with the Liberal party. (Hear, hear.) No doubt there is a division in their ranks, but speaking now for the great mass of the Irish Nationalists I say this, they have grasped—the Irish democracy has grasped—the hand of the English democracy that was stretched out to it in friendship. They would not let it go at the bidding of the greatest leader that the Irish race ever had and are not going to let it go at the bid- ding of smaller men. (Hear, hear.) I pass, there fore, from that topic, and go on to the next of those constitu- tional questions which are suggested by the Liberal programme premulgated in Newcastle, and the next of them is the DURATION OF PARLIAMENTS. (Hear, hear.) At one time it might have been supposed that the septennial period of the duration of Parliament could only give rise to what I may call a speculative abuse, that that period would never be used by any. Government fel. the purpose of keeping together a Par- liament that was completely out of touch with the con- stituents, but we have got in the action of the present Government an object lesson in that—(bear, hear)—be- cause they have not only kept the present Parliament together long after it had ceased to be in touch with the constituencies, but, judging from what we see occa- sionally in the papers, especially lb an article I think in last Monday's "Standard," they would seem disposed to keep it together to the very last moment of the seven years. Now, that is a crying abuse ; it is an abuse which calls for a remedy, and which will receive it, and I shall cordially support any proposition for reducing the sep- tennial period to a period which will enable the beneficial work of Parliament to be carried on. It is hard to say what that period exactly should be. Some people have suggested three years and some five, but I have no doubt that, whenever the question is fully and carefully considered a period will be determined upon which,while it will not unduly harass with repeated general elections and will not prevent efficient work being done, yet at the same time will prevent such a scandal as exists at the present moment when the present Parliament is still in being, notwithstanding that it has completely lost the confidence of the nation. (Applause.) The next question I shall touch upon just very briefly is that of a very august assembly, THE HOUSE OF LORDS. (Hear, hear and laughter.) That is very shortly put in the programme—the "mending or ending" of the House of Lords; only the matter of a letter. (Laughter.) With regard to the House of Lords they were once very well described by a gentleman, who is now a Unionist, Mr. Goschen. He described them as a permanent high Tory Committee, and a capital description it was. (Laughter.) Why, they are more Tory than the Tories themselves. They, instead of being an aid to legisla- tion in any shape or form, have been simply an obstacle and an impediment to legislation. Every single reform, almost I may say, without exception, has been carried by the House of Commons in spite of them. If they took any question, whether it was an extension of the franchise, whether it was relieving labourers from the restraints that were placed upon combination, whether it was a question of protecting women and children in mines or in places where they were exposed to dangers, no matter what reform, educational, social, economic, or otherwise, they would find that the House of Lords gave to that reform its most obstinate hostility. (Hear, hear.) Therefore, the question that would have to be considered is, what are you to do with them? Can you reform them? (" No" and laughter.) Well, you know to a certain extent the experiment has been tried, because Liberals to the number of hundreds have been added to the House of Lords within I think the last 60 years and the heirs at law of those Liberal lords have become iiist as Tory as if they were descen- dants of the Crusaders. (Laughter.) Although lam a Radical. I am not personally anxious to see ancient institutions destroyed if they can be improved and made beneficially, to work. (Hear, hear.) But, as I have said before, if this institution and the House of Lords cannot be mended why then it must be ended. ("That's it" and applause.) And as far as I see "it never would be missed." (Laughter.) You see if all the beneficial legislation that has been effected has been really carried by the House of Commons with the opposition of the House of Lords, what do we want with a second chamber at all? That is how the thing presents itself to my mind, but I am not a bigoted reformer at ,all, and if a feasible scheme for reforming the House of Lords could be devised, and if that scheme was con- sistent with real and effective legislation, why I for my part would not have any rooted objection to retaining that august body. (Hear, hear.) Another matter that is suggested by this programme is one of considerable importance, having regard to the electorate, and it is that of

REGISTRATION AND ELECTORAL REFORM. Now, with regard to registration. I do not think it will be necessary for me in Warrington to elaborate that point at all. You all know the difficulties which work- ing-men have to exercise the franchise. You know that, in fact, owing to the difficulty created by re- movals, under the present state of the law, practically a large number of the working-classes are absolutely disfranchised. And although working-men are the larger sufferers by this, yet they are not the only suf- ferers. Many other peopleonany other capable citizens, find themselves disfranchised, 3ust in the same way. A curious case came under my notice the other day,one of a Methodist clergyman, who had never been able to exercise the franchise, owing to the fact that, according [ to some regulations in his church, clergymen are moved about from district to district, for some wise purpose which the rulers of that church of course are perfectly competent to determine upon, but being moved about from place to place in that way he never was able to exercise the franchise at all. I have no doubt that was only a typical instance of what must have occurred with a great number of his brethren. Therefore, where an abuse of that kind exists, and where the remedy is so easy and BO simple as it is—uy the alteration of the regis- tration laws, there ought to be, at all events, neither doubt nor hesitation in applying that remedy. (Cries of "hear, hear.") Another matter, of course, about which there can be equally little doubt is ONE MAN ONE TOTE. (Applause.) The idea that the legitimate electorate of the constituency should be swamped by outsiders, as is often the case, and that probably the election which is now very close should turn upon the votes of people who have no connection with the constituency for any practical purpose, that is really an abuse which cannot be allowed any longer to remain. (Ap- plause.) Therefore the principle of one man one vote should always have my cordial support. (Applause.) Another matter to which I would wish to call your attention very shortly is one in which the work- ing classes are very much interested. I think we are all pretty well convinced that if you want to legislate for any class you must have advice and have [ information from that class at first hand. (Cries of " Hear, hear.") There was a time when an idea was abroad that people did not know anything about their own business—(a laugh)—and that if you wanted to im- prove an individual's condhion you were not to go near him and to ask him what he would propose,you were not to ask that man who wore the shoe where it pinched, but you were to form your own ideas upon the subject and give effect to them without any regard either to his wishesor to his views. But that idea is now happily exploded—(hear hear)—and one of the principles which has been adopted by the Liberal party is that if we are to legislate upon questions relating to working-men we ought to have WORKING-31EN REPRESENTATIVES. (Applause.) Now, , of course, one of the difficulties about having ques- tionworkHing.tinheenarrereAseTilitealetelvteiosnisist,hneotwith of expense. (ea • standing that of recent years much has been done to reduce the expense, an expensive matter, and there is an irreducible minimum below which the expense can- net be reduced. But one suggestion, and, I think 'a most valuable suggestion it is, is that the expenses of the returning officers should, at all events, be borne out of the rates, and in that way one expense, at least, of an election would be reduced, and one of the difficulties of the introduction of working-men representatives into Parliament would be diminished. (Hear, hear.) Now, of course a working-man sitting in Parliament is de- prived while he is in Parliament of the ordinary means of earning a livelihood, consequently another, and a very practical and very excellent suggestion is made, and one that would receive my support, and that is the recogni- tion of the principle, at all events, of the payment of members. (Applause.) Within what limits that should be recognised is a matter of detail which I think there would be no difficulty in afterwards adjusting. (Hear, hear.) Now, the next matter that I wish to say a word about, it'd it is perhaps the last of this group of consti- tutional questions which I have alluded to, is the DISESTABLismarRNT AND DisENDOwmENT of certain churches, at all events, and the applicatimn of he property of.these churches to public purposes. Now,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 9 189?.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 9 189?.

it is pleasant to find that as regards one of these churches at any rate we have theemroval of Mr. Chamberlain. (Laughter.) We only differ from him on one poieft. He thinks that the right way to go about disestablishing the church in Wales is to keep the Tories in office. (Laugh- ter.) Well,l am bound to say that the Tories don't seem to think so. (Laughter.) I think they have given him a pretty broad hint that he had better drop that out of his programme. But it is really amusing almost to think that Mr. Chamberlain would ever have gravely pro- ponnded the proposition that Tories were prepared to disestablish any church. (Laughter.) Fortunately upon this question of disestablishment and disendowment you have, at all events, the guidance and the encouragement which are afforded by tho result of the experiment as tried in my country. (Hear, hear.) We have dis- establishment in Ireland—you, for us, have disestablished the Irish church ; and it was done with a due regard to private endowments ; and it was done without inflicting any hardship whatever upon individuals. Moreover, think that the experience of Irish disestablishment proves this, that neither the interests of true re- ligion nor the interests of the particular form of establishment concerned have suffered by the change. The members of the episcopal church of Ire- land, the hierarchy of the clergy and the laity, with commendable zeal and remarkable skill, set about reorganising their church, aud they 'have succeeded completely, and so far from their church having suffered by the change, I do believe that owing to the greater interest the laity now take in the church, the episcopal body is really in a more healthy condition than it ever was at any previous time. (Applause.) Of course I need not say that the application of the property which formerly belonged to the church far purposes of public utility has been of the greatest service in Ireland. Therefore it is that I, with all the more confidence, am prepared to vote for the disestablishment of the church in Wales and the disestablishment of the church in Scotland. . (Hear, hear.) We will say nothing at present about the • disestablishment of the church in England. {Rear hear.)

Now, sir, I pass on from this question to One or two others which are of great moment, but some of which I shall be obliged to only spend a minute or two upon. i Now, the first s the question of FREE EDUCATION. Now, sir, with regard to that, fortunately the principle of free education has been adopted (hear hear) and all that remains for Liberals is to see that that system which has been so encouraged, and so established shall be brought to as great perfection as possible. (Hear hear.) -Of course the great thing will be to see that all schools that are supported by public money shall be subject to public control. (Loud applause.) Other improvements of course remain to be made, but that would appear to me, to be the principal matter, and probably would bring all those in its train. Now, sir, the next matter is one on which I shall trouble you with a few more observations than I have been able to make about the last and that is the question of

TEMPERANCE LEGISLATION. (lapplause.) Now, sir, lam in favour of a popular veto upon the drink traffic—(hear, hear, and applause) —and while I say that, I wish in the first place to make this observation, that I think great care must be taken not to expect too much from legislative restrictions of that kind. I believe that the sources of intemperance are very wide and very deep. I believe that misery and discomfort, sorrow and suffering, vice and ignorance, loneliness and ennui are great incentives to drunkenness —(hear, hear)—and I believe therefore that if you want really to grapple with this evil, you must at the same time that you adopt restrictive measures see that you get at the root of the thing and see that you take away these incentives to intemperance which I have just mentioned. (Applause.) You must make the homes of people better —(cries of" hear, hear ")—you must im- prove their education, you must give them means of wholesome recreation—(hear, hear,)—and you must give them opportunities of social intercourse. (Re- newed hear, hears.) And I think if you do both these things, apply your restrictive measures and at the same time redress these evils under which the masses of people are labouring, you will very probably get over the great drink difficulty. But yeu are not to suppose fora moment that I underrate the importance of legislation upon this subject. Experience proves that restrictive mea- sures have a most important and powerful effect in reducing the amount of drunkenness in the country. Now I don't know whether any of you are aware—pro- bably some of you are—of the experiment that has been tried, and successfully tried, in Norway and Sweden. It is generally called I think TR@ GOTFIENBURG SYSTEM. It was originally introduced into Sweden and then it was extended to Norway, and the Norwegians improved upon the original scheme. What was done was this. Municipal Councils were given the right of granting licenses, and these licenses they never grant to private individuals at all. They grant them to societies of shareholders whose duty it is to work the monopoly they so get, in the public interest. The shareholders never get under any circumstances, no matter what the profits are, more than five per cent., and the residue of the profits are handed over to the municipal body for the purpose of being applied to benevolent objects which arer not supported out of the rates. This is the Norwegian' [improvement which has been introduced, and the reason ' was this', that in Swedan they were applied to the reduc- tion of the rates, with the result that there was rather a tendency en the part of those representing the ratepayers to encourage the making of great profits; and of course great profits could only be made by selling a great deal of drink. Well, now, that has been attended with the happiest results, especially in Norway. I may tell you I am indebted for a good deal of this informa- tion to a very valuable coatribution to this month's "Nineteenth Century," by Lord Meath. My attention was drawn to this subject a good while ago, but it was very hard to get any data to work upon. The total amount of profits over and above the five per cent. that have been made available for public ob- jects in connection with the town of Bergen alone, a town containing a population of about 60,000, shows about £78,00). It was introduced in the year 1877, so that it has been at work about 14 or 15 years, and this £78,000 has been applied to objects of public utility such as the erection of artisans', dwellings, rooms for labourers to meet in, coffee-houses, and public gardens; and amongst the rest of things they have done they have constructed a road which they call the Dram Road— (laughter)—a very fine mountain road in the neighbour- hood of Bergen, and I believe I need not explain to you why it is called Dram Road. (Renewed laughter.) You • see the temptation to force or press the sale of drink has been removed because no matter what the profits are,the shareholders can only get 5 per cent. Well, the tempt- ation, at the same time, to buy drink has been de- creased because shops in which drink is sold are by no means of an attractive character. There is none of the beauty of the gin palace about them at all, and the people who go th3re to drink are not in any way en- couraged to sit till they get drunk, and the result is that the quantity of drink consumed in Norway has been diminished. There are other regulations, such as that persons of a certain age are not allowed to be supplied , with drink at all, and I believe no barmaids are em- ployed at all. (Laughter and applause.) Well, now, sir, I think that that Is a very interesting experiment,and that seeing that it has been a very successful one, it de- serves the attention of all temperancereformers,because lyott gee it may happen that in some places the people would not veto a public-house, but would insist upon having their beer; and then it might be a veil useful thing to have an alternative plan. And such an alter- native plan appears to me to be exactly provided by this Gothenburg system. Now, sir, so much then for the temperance question. I now go on to consider some other matters of moment, passing over a couple I should have liked to speak upon but time will not permit. These are reform of the land laws—(hear, hear)—and the REFORM OF TAXATION

--- both local taxation and general taxation. I should have liked to say a word on those su'ojects, but time, as we say in the law, is of the essence of the contract, and we can only say a certain amount in a certain time. I pass them over, not because I think them unimportant but because I have something to say about another subject which will occupy time at some little length—the questions affecting the WELL-BEING OF THE WORKING CLASSES. (Hear, hear.) I should just like to make one or two general observatiohs before discussing these questions at any length, and the first is this, that all the reforms that have been introduced or will be introduced must more or less affect and improve the condition of . the working classes. Whether it is free education, or whether it is temperance legislation, or whether it is any other reform in which the community at large participate, working- men must participate, and must participate largely,and although it may be that tha present generation of work- ing-men will not reap much of the benefit of it, yet no doubt the rising generation will, and working-men must ise alittle patient and wait for results. The next general observation I have to make is this, that in dealing with questions relating to the working classes we must in a large measure be guided by the working classes. kllear, hear.) Thus we must not dogmatise, but we must listen to their advice and listen to their suggestions, and listen to the information that they give us, and trying to make up our minds as best we can, getting, as I said before, our information at first hand. I think if we do that many mistakes that we have made hitherto in dealing with the working-classes will be avoided. (Hear, hear.) Just let us consider for a ' moment or two with whom it is we have to dell. We have to deal with a town population, and will have to deal with a rural population. The town population re- presents about two-thirds of the population, avid is in- creasing ; the rural population represents one-third of the population and is decreasing. Now, it is a very re- markable and unfortunate state of things. (Hear, hear.) The

in the country is less attractive still. (Hear hear.) There can be little doubt that the life of the labouring man in the country means poverty, means dependence, and means stagnation. (Hear hear.) Now, why should this be so ?

IT 73 ROT SO ABROAD, it is not so, for instance, in France. In France the pro- portions are reversed. In France about one-fourth of the population is town population, and about three- fourths rural population, and consequently it must be something in the condition of the people in France, as compared with the condition of the people in the country of England, that causes this great disparity. Now, there has been a very remarkable and a very interesting contribution to the literature of this subject published very recently by the Rev. Mr. Tuckwell—(applause)'—a man whose name will be received everywhere with the applause with which it is received in this meeting. Ile has worked immensely for the rural population in his district and all over the country. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. Mr. Tuckwell has been travelling in France, and he has had opportunity of observing there the condition of the French peasantry, and he gives an account of them and of their condition which certainly is enough, so to speak, to make our teeth water at this side of the Channel. (Hear, hear.) He describes them as being thriving and independent and hopeful and healthful,and in their old age not obliged to look forward to that dread- ful termination of their existence the workhouse. (Hear, hear.) He tells also, what is more important than all, he tens us the reason why this is so. I will give you the reason in Mr. Tuckwell's own words, because I took the precaution to cut out the contribution to the "Contemporary Review," in which it is published, for the purpose of reading it to you this evening, because 1 knew it would interest you. Every word of it is absolutely true. In describing the results of his own personal observations he goes on, "Questioning everywhere, innkeepers, wayfarers, fellow-travellers,in hotel and railway carriage, we met with unbroken testimony to the prosperity, freedom, thrift of the labouring peasants, as due to the facility of acquiring land at will and cheaply, consequent on the extinction of great landowners at the revolution' and the centrifugal distribution of the soil which followed it. The feeling is deeply rooted not only amongst the small holders but amonst the moneyed classes. To join house to house and add field to field is reprehensible with Frenchmen of to-day as was with Isaiah twenty-five cen- turies ago. Said a rich milk-dealer, who in England would have become a landlord, but whose agrarian desires were bounded by a house, garden, enclos ; " If a rich man buys an estate it is the ruin of the country, if the land is divided into parcels it is the riches of the country." And then he goes on to give us some very suggestive statistics : "ln'England the owners of estates above one acre in size are aboutr3oo,ooo; in France theyare 7,000,000. In England the average extent of a single farm is 390 acres ; in France 10 acres •, 4,000000 owners holding properties of two acres: while farms of 200 acres are so few that they can be counted on the fingers. In France there are 8,000,000 acres of common land, the exact amount which has in England been robbed from the labourers by the successive Enclosure Acts dur- ing the last 170 years. In 1880 France exported £28,000,000 worth of food ;England imported £80,000,000 worth. In 60 years 8,500.000 emigrants have left Env- land, less than 500,000 have left France. In England the rural population is 33 per cent, of the population ; in France upwards 0175 per cent. In England finally, the peasant is miserably housed, underpaid, servile des- pairing ;' in France he is decent, well-to-do, independent hopeful." " The bearings of these observations," says the immortal commander of the Cautious Clara," lies in the application of them ; that ain't part of my duty.'" (Applause.) That gives us the cause of this evil, and suggests a remedy. What we have to do IS

TO RESTORE THE LAND TO THE PEOPLE —(applause)—and the people will find their way back to the land. In that way the unhealthy over crowding to the towns and the unhealthy competition of work will be diminished, and a great many of the people in the towns I have no doubt, will be induced to go back to live a country life when a country life presents some attractions for them. That is what the Liberal party is proposing to do. It is proposing by means of allotments and by giving the people the control of their local affairs —(hear,hear)—to once more bring the people back to the country which they have deserted for the towns. And now let me read while upon that subject what the Newcastle programme says upon the subject— ., 'rhat, in the opinion of this Council, the well being of the nation no less than that of the districts immedi- ately concerned, requires that the condition of the rural population should receive the immediate attention of Parliament. The Conceit regards with satisfaction the action taken by the General Purposes Committee of the Federation, and while approving generally of the sug- gestions it has formulated, affirms as of primary impor- tance,—(a). The establishment of district and parish councils popularly elected, (b) the concession of compul- sory powers to local authorities to aquire and hold land for allotments, small holdings, village halls, places of worship, labourers dwellings, and other public purposes, (c) the reform of existing allotment acts by the removal of restrictions, by giving security of tenure, and the power to erect buildings, and the right of full compensa- tion for all improvements," (Applause.) Thai is the programme of the" Liberal party upon the subject, and by that programme I stand. (Applause.) That is what the Liberal party propose to do for the benefit of the toilers in the country, and by it they will indirectly con- fer very large benefits upon the working classes in the ' towns, but, of course, that won't satisfy tke Liberal party. The

TOILERS IN THE TOWN, as much as those in the country, have the care and solicitude of the Liberal party. They have already a splendid record of boons conferred upon the working- classes. Every great reform has been carried,initiated and carried, by them, therefore the working-classes in towns may be perfectly certain that the Liberal party will not flag in their exertions to improve their condi- tions. (Hear, hear.) It is unnecessary for me to go in minute detail into what remains to be done for them. Factory Acts, for instance, require- to be amended and extended. In other directions reforms will have to be introduced, and then, too, something must be done to ' put an end to that great evil—the necessity which the industrious, hardworking, and honest working-man has of looking, at the end of a long and laborious life, to the workhouse. (Hear, hear.) I think I have pretty well travelled over all the ground I proposed to travel over. I have endeavoured to touch upon those different sub- jects as briefly, and at the same time exhaustively, as I could.and to give you a general idea cf what my views upon them were, and IN CONCLUSION

I have only to add that, while I shall al ways support those great principles in which all the country equally is concerned, if I have the honour to be selected as yeur candidate and to be returned as your candidate at the next general election, the peculiar interests of the borough of Warrington will always find in me a zealous and, I hope, successful champion. (Loud and continued applause.)

The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried with absolute unanimity. Dr. HOUSTON, on re-entering the room was received with extraordinary enthusiasm. The Chairman stated the nature of the resolution that had been adopted and Dr. Houston, in reply, said he should ever be grateful to the Liberals of Warrington for the reception which they had given him. He felt when he came amongst them that he was amongst brothers, because they were Liberals who were working in a common cause. If he should be returned as. their representative they might regard him as pledged to maintain the views which he had laid before them and to give, in addition, special attention to the individual and peculiar interests of Warrington. (Applause.) The proceedings, which had throughout been of a most enthusiastic character, dosed with a vote of thanks to the Chairman' on the motion of Mr. Pierpoint, seconded by Mr. J. Walker, an intimation being made that an early opportunity would be taken of holding a reception with a view to introducing Dr. and Mrs. Houston to the principal workers of the Liberal party in Warrington.

div.head: DEPOPULATION OF THE RURAL DISTRICTS
div.p: DEPOPULATION OF THE RURAL DISTRICTS

has attracted the attention of politicians; they have lamented the decay of the rural population, and pro- perly so—a decay that is not confined to numbers but extends to the physique of the rural Population, at all events according to some observers. Now, the question arises, what is the cause of this? Why is the town population Increasing, and 'why is the rural population decreasing? It certainly is not that the lot of the toiler in the town is so very desirable that the country population are attracted to it, but it is that, notwith- standing all the drawbacks the life of the working- man in the town presents, the life of the labouring man

div.head: SELECTING THE CANDIDATE.
div.p: SELECTING THE CANDIDATE.

At the close of the speech the members of the press were asked to retire and they did so. The Chairman then said it was open to the meeting to question Dr. Houston on any matters as to which they Wished to be further satisfied, or to elicit further information. He was well pleased with the speech himself, and he gathered that the audience were too. (Rear, hear.) One member then asked if Dr. Houston, in case he was returned to Parliament would vote in favour of a clause being inserted in all treaties with foreign countries pro- viding for settlement by arbitation of all disputes aris- ing out of such treaties, and the answer was " Certainly." As it was evident, after a pause, that there were no other questions to be put Dr. Houston retired,to leave the Council at liberty to come to a decision in his absence. Mr. W. PIERFOINT said he was sure they had all been very much pleased, as he had, with the admirable and statesmanlike speech to which they had listened, and he had great pleasure in moving the following resolution : —" That this meeting of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association heartily thanks Dr. Houston, Q.C.,,for his address and invites him to become the Liberal candidate for the borough at the next Par- liamentary election." (Loud applause.) It was not unlikely that they would hearsomething from the oppo- site side about the nationality of their candidate but that was a thin.' which would net disturb him. He did not care whether a candidate was English, Irish, Scotch or Welsla, after he had once satisfied himself that he was an able, sound and thorough-going Liberal. (Applause.) Mr. G. Saw seconded the resolution. Councillor H. ROBERTS expressed the satisfaction with which he had listened to the speech, and said he trusted every member present would leave that room pledged to render all the assistance that he possibly could to ensure the return of Dr. Houston. He sometimes felt ashamed of Warrington when lie thought of the way in which it was represented, but the opportunity would be afforded before lore, of redeeming the political representation of the borough, and it was their duty to make the best use of that opportunity. (Applause.) Mr. T. BIRCHALL spoke in a similar strain, and referred to his satisfaction at seeing a member of the Rylands' family in the person of their president presiding over that meeting. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. F. LouonLlN said they might be prepared for mean and underhand attacks upon their candidate and slights upon his character and nation, though the Tories had nothing to say about a speaker being an Irishman when he happened, like Dr. Renton', to be a Tory. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Councillor F. A. ROBERTS' C.C., said that, as late chairman of the executive, he was conscious of the time that had elapsed in securing a candidate,but he thought now that they saw the result they would say it had not been lost. He was pleased to think that he had been the means of mentioning Dr. Houston to members of the executive and he might assure them that, although he was not now a voter in Warrington, he would render all the assistance he could in the election campaign. (Ap- plause.) Mr. J. Price and Mr. J. Pemberton expressed their sat- isfaction on behalf of the working-class element with the straightforward and sympathetic manner in which Dr. Houston had dealt with questions which were of special interest to workingmen,

RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. LANCASTER. rotlowing their hard match with Wigan on New Year's, Day, the Warringtonians journeyed to Lancaster on Saturday, where they encountered the leading club of
that town for the first time this season. It was a clanger-
ous experiment to ask the team to undergo two such
difficult matches in such a short period, for it is an ac- knowledged fact that Lancaster possesses as strong a set ot forwards as any team in the north. Taking thematch
with Wigan, which was a hard forward _battle, it is no

wonder the team was not quite so fresh as one could wish. The visitors were still without Smack Bate, whilst Lancaster had whipped together their strongest 15% In consequence of the high wind, the game was divided _
into four quarters. and Warrington had the advantage of the slope and wind in the initial opening. Play at the
outset was at the half way flag, where some exchanges between Heesnm, Boscow, and Bleasdale, eventually saw

Webster snapping up a chance, and dash dawn the open until he was hauled down about ten yards from the line. This gave the visitors a footing, which they maintained, for a lengthened period, and the first to try and utilize the advantage were Bate and Holmes, who led up to the line, only to be repulsed by Lambert. Some fine work by the Warrington forwards was productive of Ashton crossing the line, but a miscalculation by the referee of the scorer and Handles negatived the point—hard lines for Warrington. Front the scrimmage ordered, Lan- caster relieved lightly, but Jolley, Turner, Donohue, and Thorniley soon had the oval back again. Smart passing of Lancaster enabled them to reach the quarter flag, but prompt as had been the relief so was the return to the attack. Lancaster tackled vigorously, and rarely missed their men, and where one failed to accomplish his desired purpose, he was readily joined by a host of his comrades. Play was at half way when Turner had.. a kick by way of penalty, and the oval was landed at the home lines once more. Nevins and Bate now passed well, but Hartley tackled Evans finely, and disaster was avoided. By degrees the oval was worked away, and travelled to Boscow, who gave his side the advan- tage of attacking by a fine kick into touch at the quarter flag. The visiting backs indulged in a series of transfers, only to find the movement upset la 7 the strict attention of Bleasdale and Lambert. From scrimmage near the line, Nevins dashed through th thick of his opponents, being held under the posts. Cowell next made his mark, but the relief was tempor- ary, and when the first quarter had ended not a score had been made. On turning round, Evans was the first to show up, with a rnn along the popular side, Cowell tackling him well. A fine kick by Lambert sent the oval to the Warrington 22, but if the defence of Lan- caster in the first half was staunch, so was that set up by Warrington. Boscow was compelled to save from a rush. The play was at half way, when Nevins,Holmes, Berry, and Jolley helped to invade the Lancaster ground, and Cowell being harassed on one occasion, the visitors did not utilize a chance which might have decided the 1 fortunes of the day. Lancaster, favoured by this luck,.] now went away, and some passing between the backs was deserving of the applause it elicited. The effort was futile, for Webster and Heesom were all there. Again, Warrington showed up with some loose dribbling but Hanby retaliated, and Gibson making his mark in response to a kick by Boscow, the place taken by 13Ieas- dale sent up the second minor. A passing run by Jolley and Evans saw the Lancaster lines threatened once more but the attack was brief, for judicious kicking by Hart- I ley and Cowell raw Boscow defending his lines in clever style. No further score was made up to half time, when Lancaster were leading by two minors. Lancas- ter were the attacking party immediately after the kick off, but Holmes got clear from some loose play, but dallied too long with the oval for anything substantial to result from the effort. Cowell foiled him, but Webs- ter, Bate, Heesom, and Donohue headed a movement to the line, the latter being held on the verge of scoring. Nevins, Bate, and Evans passed neatly,. but the latter was firmly held, and after a brilliant rush by the home forwards had been saved by Heesom, a bad pass to I Webster spoiled a certain score. Hartley endeavoured to getaway, but Boscow had the measure of him, and 1 a too strict attention of the visiting half backs I saw Nevins taking a place kick by way of penalty, the wind spoiling a fine attempt, Warrington experienced hard lines again a moment later, for the game was suspended when Jolley, Holmes,. and Berry had worked the oval past all opposition,.the stoppage being brought about by two home players hav- ing collided. Again Jolley and A.sliton got away, but the third quarter saw ends being changed with no tangible score on the sheet. Starting the last quarter, Warrington went about their work with such a will that at once threatened the home -citadel. A kick by Heesom placed Warrington on the aggressive, and a dribble by Berry caused Cowell' to save. Some faulty passing by Warrington backs gave relief ,and Webster saved his lines twice. The visitors returned to the attack once more,but Hartley intercepted a'pass from Turner, and ran clear down the open, the run realizing a try by Kitchen, Bleasdale failing at the place. With only a few minutes to play, the game was considered as good as over, but Bate get clear, for Holmes to knock on. Handles Turner, and Holmes again passed well, and a last effort by Ashton saw him being pull3d down near the line, and a hard fought game concluded—Lancaster, 0-1-2 ; Warrington, 0-0-1. Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back; Evans, Hee- som, and Webster,.three-quarter backe ; J. T. Bate, and 1 Nevins, half-backs; Ashton, Turner Jolley, Donohue,, Thorniley, Handles, Berry, Teare, and Flolmes,forwards. Lancaster: Cowell, back ; Hartley, Bleasdale, and Lam- bert, three-quarters ;. Hanby and Garth half-backs ; Herbert Stephenson, Winder, Kitchen, Roberts, Thomp- son, Lofthouse, Gibson, and Weir. WARRINGTON " A " v. LANCASTER " A."—This encoun- ter was played at Warrington in wretched weather, the ground being very heavy going. Lancaster, winning the toss, took advantage of the elements,, and quickly forced the home team on the defensive, until Sampson cleared finely. This was followed by Daniels dribbling to neutral territory, but the strong loose play indulged in by the Lancastrians carried hostilities right to the line, and a minor was conceded. Following the drop out, Bailey, by a clever movement, tried to break through, but Gardiner got a free kick into dangerous position for the home team. Nothing came of the oppor- tunity, and Barnes, Daniels, and Lally were instrumental in removing the scene of operations to more desirable quarters. Directly after this another minor was con- ceded to the visitors. Sampson effected a fine clearance of his lines. Warrington, headed by Davies, Barnes, Rowlands,. and Warburton, getting the ball at their toes were well into their opponents' lines, when a foolish kick enabled Lambert to regain all the lost ground. The visiting forwards were playing strongly, but some pass- ing by them lost ground, and Philips, Forster, Isher- wood, and Hampson got away to the centre line. Fly kicking by the north men renewed the pressure, until Davies, Bailey, Barnes, and Rowlands forced the leather Ito the quarter flag. A smart bit of play by Barnes was supplemented by a grand piece of work by Antrobus and Bailey, the running being taken up by Warburton, Sampson, and Rowlands. The attack was but brief, for the ball was rushed into the home ground, where a kick was followed up by Parry, who scored by the posts, which was easily converted. Lally then dribbled finely, which enabled Warrington to press for a time, until a bad past allowed Gardiner to make rapid tracks for the line, And Warrington were in turn defenders. Daniels and Barnes broke through to relieve a heavy pressure, and half-time arrived with Lancaster 1 goal 2 minors to nil. With the wind at their backs, Warrington took the ball grandly in the loose to the line, Lally getting finely away and a try seemed certain, but Daniels was. safely held, and a minor conceded. A rush, headed by Warburton, Phillips, Hampson, and Forster, nul- lified the drop out, but a strong kick sent the leather dead. Lancaster, through the efforts of Barnes and Daniels were severely pressed, and the last-named at length scored, Sampson making a grand attempt. By some vigorous forward play, Ralph Leen- ing and Parr carried the operations to the llama 25 ; but the stay was of short duration, as Potts by a tricky piece of play gained a lot of ground. Warrington attacked strongly, and fully tested the tackling powers of the Lancastrians. Antrobus and Potts then showed a fine display of passing and re-passing, and the ball be- ing taken over, Davies scored. Immediately afterwards Barnes started a loose rush, which baffled the visitors, Davies securing another try. Free kicks to either side ensued, and Forster, Isherwood, Hampson, and Phillips dribbled to the line for Lally to obtain a fourth try. Lancaster then had another look in, Putts and Sampson saving splendidly, and while the outlook was ominous, and play waging under the goal, Davies and Potts effected a grand relief ttransferring the game to midfield, the whistle blowing with Warrington 0.4-3 to 141-8..

NOSE ALMOST COT OFF. At the borough police court,on Thursday,before Alder- men Francomb and Harrison,Sarah Bennett,wife of John, , Bennett,. employed by the Cheshire Lines Committee and living at 10, Vere-street, was charged with wilfully and. maliciously doing grievous bodly harm to Thos. Alfred James, litter. also employed by the Cheshire Lines Coin-, ' mittee and living at 28, Crossley-street, by striking him, with alighted paraffin lamp on Sunday night, . about a quarter pasteleven.—Thos. Alfred James, who appeared with his nose plastered up and was so weak that he had to be accommodated with a seat, gave evidence. The prisoner's husband, he said, came to his (witness's)honse on Saturday last and stayed with him till Sunday night. They went out, and, coming back, found the prisoner at the house. She commenced beating her husband. Wit- ness tried to make peace between them, and he opened the door with the intention of putting the prisoner out. She took the lighted lamp off the table and hit witness with it, and as she did so it broke into pieces and fell on the floor. He had had no previous quarrel with the prisoner. He was very friendly with her husband. Witness had had some drink, but was not drunk.—Mary James, the prosecutor's wife, who had a plaster under one ef her eyes, said the prisoner came into the com- plainant's,house. She had had some drink. She enquired for her husband, using bad language about him and threatening what she would do to him when she was sober. She said "I will give it him, stopping out all night. Witness's husband and the prisoner's husband came back while theprisoner was in and Mr. James told her to make a less noise or else go out. He tried to put her out,.but could not get the door open, and she then struck him with the lighted lamp, across the face. The force of the blow broke the lamp and put it out- Wit- ness went out for help and when she canie back the pri- soner was. outside. Mr. James was 'fainting with his head on the table, and bleeding from the nose, which was hanging by a bit of skin. He was taken to the In- firmary.—Mary Rabbit,a lodger at the prosecutor's,gave corroborative evidence, and said after the blow he was lying on the floor.—P.C. Jones said he went into Jame' house at 10. minutes to 12 p.m. on the night in question, hearing a noise coming from it, and found him with his face covered with blood. The point of his nose was hanging down to his mouth. The floor and the wall were covered with blood and glass ; and the place looked like a slaughterhouse. He bandaged the prosecutor's nose up and,, with assistance, took him to the Infirmary, first taking the prisoner to the Polme Station. She was three parts drunk.—Dr. Bowden, of the Infirmary, deposed that the nose had almost been cut off and the prosecutor might lose it entirely.—The prisoner was committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions the magistrates con- senting to accept two sureties of each as bail. THE DOBCTIOM DISEASES ACT.---APPLICATION BY TAB TOWN CLERK. At the Bbrough Police Court on Thursday Mr. J. Lyon Whittle,: town clerk, applied to the Bench for an order to remove a child, daughter of Alice Peers, of 9,. Haraii- ton-st., from her home where she was suffering from scarlet fever, and there were several other children, to the infectious diseases hospital. The mother of the child objected strongly to its removal, but this was necessary in the opinion of the Medical Officer (Dr. Gomel!) for-the purpose of isolating the disease. Evi- dence having been given by Mr. Bloomfield in support of the application, it was acceded to. The Mayor, who presided, said he could not understand parents obj ect- ing to their children going to the hospital under such circumstances. The child received every possible care, and was placed in a magnificent building and properly isolated and attended to night and day, free •of charge. The mother could come to see the child if she chose.. He believed in almost every case where a child had been in the hospital it was most anxious to go back. He was sure the treatment the children received there was quite as good as at home. Hoes? DEALER CHARGED WITH SWINDLING .A JEW. Sohn W. Goodwin, home dealer, was charged with obtaining by false pretences on the 2nd ult.' a gold albert watch guard from Mark Steinart, for the arm of Aaronson and Steinart, of Manchester. The' prosecutor said on tit, 2nd of Decomber, he was intro- duced to the prisoner at the Rose and Crown.lnn, by the the landlord's wife, who said " Here is a customer for you. He has plenty of money." The prisoner told him his name was John James Goodwin, and gave his address as 13 Cairo-street. He said he wanted a gold albert and he let him have one worth £l3, the prisoner saying that he would pay so much on the 28th of December, and the remainder a fortnight later, He went to Cairo-street to find him but there was no number IS, He heard no more of him till he was apprehended by the police at Preston. Abel Rushworth, landlord of the Rose and Crown, deposed to his wife introduoing to Mr. Steinart, the prisoner, who was in the habit of stabling horses on witness's premises. She said she had known the prisoner for three weeks' and she thought he was in a good position-- the defendant said the address he gave the prosecutor was 29,. Cairo-st., where he had lodged with a widow, but on being asked by Alderman Sutton he could nct tell her name.—Mr. Rushworth, in reply to the prisoner, said he remembered his address, being advertised as 29, Cairo-st., but that address could not be found.—The prisoner pleaded' not guilty, and offered to pay so much a month for the chain.—Alder- man Sutton : No, that won't do, because you are here, there, and everywhere. He might never see you again. —The prisoner having had £9 2s. a found upon him when arrested, the prosecutor said he would accept £9 now and the remainder after.—Alderman Sutton said the Bench could not compromise the matter between the, parties.—The prisoner offered to. pay half the amount down and the-remainder after.--The Bench considered/ the case not proved, and dismissed it.—Goodwin said he Would pay the prosecutor a pound or two now.—The Chief Constable : You offered to pay him half just now.. You are a shuffier. AN APRRENTICE.DETAINRD* A.T THE BARRACKS.. At the Borough Police Court; yesterday morning,, the case of Colonel A. C. Twentvenan, C.8.V.C.,_ was summoned to show, cease why he should not deliver up an apprentice, aged 19 years, who was detained at the Orford Barracks,having joined the army.—Mr. Garner, solicitor, of St. Helens, appeared for the lad's employes, and stated that he was apprenticed to Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, of that place, in February, 1888, for six, years and four months,,the indenture expiring next Sone, He had absconded, and been discovered at Orford Barracks. Mr. Garner having himself given formal evidence to prove the case, an order was made for thedad to be delivered up.

div.head: PROPOSED PUBLIC MEETING IN EARLES-
div.p: PROPOSED PUBLIC MEETING IN EARLES-
TOWN.

Sir,—Several letters have appeared of late in the local papers in regard to the proposed Earlestown Public Hall and the excessive expense which that Hall is likely to entail on the district. As I see little prospect of any benefit likely to accrue from such correspondence, I would suggest that a public meeting be called for an early date, when the subject can be thoroughly dis- cussed, the views of the ratepayers ascertained, and conveyed (by a deputation chosen at that meeting) in unmistakable terms to the Commissioners at their next general meeting. Thus, if the district is to be saddled with a heavy burden it will be of our own choosing and With our full consent, and with the satisfaction of know- ing that each and all have had the full opportunity of expressing their feelings on so important a subject. I leave to the Ratepayers' Association the arrangement of details as to time, place, and Chairmanship of the sug- gested meeting, and remain, Sir, your obedient servant, AN INTERESTED RATEPAYER. Earlestown, Jan. 6th, 1892.

Sir,—That the correspondence anent the prwosed Public Hall is interesting to your readers is evidenced by a number of questions which are being very gener- ally discussed at the present time. Below I venture to give a few of the most amusing. 1. At the next election how many railway men will be elected?
2. Could the town be worse served than at present ? 3. Flow much will Mr. Ratcliffe's property be in- creased in value by the erection of the Public Hall ?

4. Estimating, the extra rate at one shilling in the £, how much will the Railway Company have to pay for the Public flail? 5. Seeing that the Railway Company have the large hall at the Viaduct Institute what benefit will their workmen derive from the Public Hall? 6. Will Mr. Thonspson be a silent member? 7. Do one-third of the Torch Light Processionists pay rates? 8. How many actual ratepayers desire this large expenditure on a Public Hail? 9. Should not a poll be taken ? 10, If a meeting be called how many speeches will Blue Bottle make? U. Excepting the yew ratepayers who have property in close proximity to it, whom will the Public Hall benefit? 12. Will the ratepayers allow themselves to be gulled in this Public Hall question? A number of others could be put, but perhaps the above will be sufficient for the present. If one of your correspondents will be good enough to reply in your next issue,the education of the ratepayers would,l think, be further forwarded. ENQUIRER.
January 5, 1892.
LET US lIAVE A CIRCUS.
Sir,—The now classical saying of our noble Premier has taken firm hold of my imagination. I say by all means

let us have a circus! It is a kind of ring I can fully appre- ciate, which is not the case with some other rings we wot of—syndicates of this, that, or the other—the outcome of selfishness with a product of misery. I like— for this is a letter on personal predilections—l like to bear the clown crack his jokes to the crack of the riding- master's whip—he is what he appears to be, and often something more. But my Lord the Marquis, notwithstanding, we cannot always be in the circus. So thing the Liberals of Warrington, and as an outcome of the thought they have chosen a very good candidate and one who may show the noble marquis that buffoonery is not the need of the hour. I hope our candidate is a presentable man, that is from:the ladies' point of view. It is highly desirable that he should not only be osculate- able but osculatory. He should be kissable and fond of kissing ; this is of great importance in a constituency like ours. They say kissing goes by favour. Here it goes by favours. He should be thoroughly domesticated, that is he should be able to control any outward mani- festation of disgust when dangling the little popsy- wopsies of his female admirers. Among his other gifts rhe should have a turn for the mangle. As one good turn deserves another, this might serve to turn him into an M.P. It will be a sad disappointment to the ladies with politically osculatory propensi- ties if our candidate can not be brought to see that the grasping of a political idea includes the embrac- ing of the candidate. For the last decade I have been wondering why we need trouble ourselves about electing a member for our town, seeing we got along so well without a representative, but the above considerations convince me that something more is wanted. Of course I do not regard an M.P. as being a remedy for all the ills of life. He is only a specific not an uni- versal panacea. In fine he is not like the patent medi- cine which so much relieved the man who could not breath under an umbrella, and which the wag said was the only remedy enabling him to breath under the canopy of heaven. Herein we may see that there are other uses to which a Parliamentary representative might advantageously be put. Let our electors see to it.—l am, ,kc., 'EERS.
JOHN P)
