I thought it extremely probable that one who held so tenaciously the belief in man's gradual evolution from the animal would be prepared to contend for the gradual evolution of the animal from organised living matter, and the latter from inorganic materials. It is our logical process throughout. Mr. Peers wishes to begin the discussion on the top storey of this living structure. No ! I will meet him at the foundations. A few words more and then I finish. In my first letter

I v-z.rOte a's-f-o-11-cTeVS-:=-" If the whole of living nature, and the whole domain of mind are to be referred to purely material causes then there is no longer room or reason for God, matter being a sufficient explanation of all things." Mr. Peer in quoting the above suppressed the passage in italics. The statement as it stands is the expression of a truth well nigh self-evident to most minds, viz : That if matter can explain everything, then as a mere affair of logic there 19 no occasiox for a God. " But may not Liod be required to explain matter ?" Yes, this inference is quite admissible, but its validity will be denied by the Atheist, the Monist, the Agnostic, and by Evolutionists of the type of Biichner and Hieckel. "As science advances the man-formed-idea of God recedes,but commensurate with the recession the idea is ennobled and enlarged." The advance of science then enables and enlarges our idea of God ; and "the phil- osopher who cannot even conceive the idea " is very unscientific indeed, even though that philosopher be none other than Mr. John Peers.—l am yours truly, W. H. BUTLER. Wilderspoel.

Sir,—Tho usual demand note has just been left at my house, and I am therein advised that I have to pay threepence in the pound as highway rate. Now, I am not a gentleman, nor the son of a gentleman, if you take the term in its commen acceptation, and regard those only as gentlemen" who do nothing, and have plenty to help them," or as another said—" Those who sow not and who spin not." Not being a gentleman in this sense, I cannot afford to keep either carriage or horses, nor am lin a position whenever I may need to visit Warrington to order a cab; but I am a good pedestrian, and the 'distance to Watrington is not far. But why should my limbs and life be imperilled through the carelessness of others whom I help to pay to do :a cer- tain work?

CLOSING OF THE VITRIOL DAY AND SUNDAY SCHOOL. On Sunday afternoon the scholars attending the Vitriol Sunday School,which has been conducted in accordance with the Church of England principles, assembled for tuition for the last time, in conse- quence of the Sankey Sugar Co., having intimated that they did not intend to any longer maintain it as either a day or Sunday school. The school not being a certified institution,and receiving no grant from Government, has for a good number of years been maintained by the Sankey Sugar Co., far the benefit primarily of the children of their employes, but other children were not debarred from attending. The attendance before the Free Education Act came into force was something like 100 daily, but immediateiy up- on the Act coming into operation, and the opening of the new Church of Engladd schools in Market-Fe..., the attendance very materially decreased, until only about 20 children's names appeared upon the books. The Sankey Sugar Co, naturally resented the great falling off in the attendance, which they asserted was premature, the parents of the children haying removed the latter to other schools before they were aware of what action the Sankey Sugar Company would take in consequence of the Free Educa- tion Act. With such a meagre attendance, the services required from the schoolmistress were practically nil, and the pecuniary assistance derived from the fee being altogether inadequate, the Sankey Company decided to abandon the day school, and as such it has been closed for about a month. It therefore followed as a natural consequence that the Sunday School would also have to go to the wall, as the Sankey Co. refused any further support, and on Sunday afternoon the Rev. E. J. Hack, curate of Wargrave Church, had the unpleasant task of announcing the fact. The Sunday School has been es- tablished, and been in active work for a little over 16 years, the number of scholars on the books being 106, and its closing comes as a great blow to those who have been so long and intimately connected with it. The scene on Sunday afternoon, when the Superintendent (Mr. E. Burrows) and the teachers bade each other fare- well was of a touching description. Mr. Hack, in mak- ing the announcement to the scholars explained to them the reason for ohe step taken by the Sankey Sugar Corn parry, and at the same time said that their thanks were due to the Sankey Company, for the kindness they had displayed, since the establishment of the school, towards the officials connected with it, and also for the support they had afforded. Mr. E. Burrows (Superintendent), regretted exceed- ingly the closing of the school, but he advised the chil- dren not to forsake their principles, but to stick to some Church of England School. Each child on leaving the school was presented with a Bible or Testament, and the Superintendent shook hands with the children, bidding them farewell. SHOCKING RAILWAY FATALITY AT NEWTON. A sad accident, having a fatal termination, befel a young fellow, 10 years old, named William G. Blackmore, belonging to Edge Hill, and employed as a porter at Newton-le-willows Station, on Sat- urday night. Blackmore lodged with Mr. Samuel Dalies in Mercer street, Newton, and had been r Newton Bridge Station about six months. The 4-5. p.m. passenger train from Liverpool runs to Newton- le-Willows, calling at all stations on the way. When it reaches Newton, and after discharging its passengers, it runs on to Parkside, and then backs down over the crossings at Lowton junction station, afterwards proceeding round the Lowton curve to Newton Bridge, where the coaches are placed in a siding until next morning; but the engine runs on to Earlestown to work the 7-29 p.m. train to Wigan. On Saturday night this work was carried out as usual, Blackmore accompanying the train for the purpose of seeing to the lamps, Scc. The train had backed down to Lowton junction, and stopped about 30 yards outside the station, when Blackman got down, and went behind the last carriage for rho purpose of altering the slide in the tail lamp. Whilst he was engaged doing this, owing to some misunderstanding, the engine set back, and whether the deceased was knocked down by the carriages, or fell in trying to get out is not quite clear, but the fact remains that he fell across the rails, and the carriage wheels passed over his body. Another porter named Fred Jenkinson, who was in the train, heard Blackman cry out, and im- mediately signalled to the driver to stop. Jenkinson and the driver (Gardener) then went to the spot, and found Blackman on the rails quite conscious, as on see- ing Jenkinson, he said, "Oh, Fred, I'm killed," and im- mediately afterhe said, • Fred, I'm dead." Jenkinson and Gardener picked him up, and found that the wheels had passed over the groins, and almost severed both legs. They placed him in a carriage and took him to Newton Bridge. Dr. Watkins was in attendance, and pronounced life to be extinct,and the body was removed to the Legh Arms Hotel, to await the inquest. THE INQUEST. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy-coroner, held an inquiry at the Legh Arms Hotel, Newton, on Tuesday afternoon, Into the circumstances attending the death of William George Brackmare, who was killed as stated above. Mr. Bland from the solicitor's office, Lime-st., represented the London and North-Western Railway Company. Thomas Blackmore, a gardener living at 21 Lear-road, Edge Hill, Liverpool, said the deceased, William George Blackmore, was his son. He was a porter on the Lon- don and North-Western Railway at Newton-le-Willows, and was 18 years of age last November. He lodged with Mr. Davies at 98 Mercer-st., Newton. Frederick Jenkinson, a porter at Newton-le-Willows station, said he knew the deceased, who had been a por- ter at the station, between six and seven months. On the 2nd inst., he was with deceased in the 4.50 train from Liverpool, at Parkside, and it would then be about six o'clock in the evening. Witness was in the yan,and deceased was changing the tail light slide at the back of the van, preparatory to the train shunting back on to the Liverpool curve, to go to Newton-le-Willows. While he was changing the light, the train was stationary and then began to move back. Witness heard the carriages next the van jolt, and he immediately applied the vacuum and stopped the train. He then went out, and found deceased under the second carriage from the van, with his legs across the rails, and he had been run over. Be was alive when witness got to him, but he died two or three minutes afterwards.—The Coroner: Who sig- nalled on the train 7—Witness It must have been the pointsma.n.—The Coroner : You did'nt.—Witness : No Sir! I had no lamp at all.—/n ansner to Sergeant Long- worth, witness said the train was stationary when de- ceased got out ef the train at Lowton, and he had witness's hand lamp with him.—Sergeant Longworth : Had he altered the tail lamp at all I"—Witness : The tail lamp was off altogether, and was thrown on one side, together with witness's hand lamp. They were within three yards from where deceased was lying. Francis Gardiner, said he was driver of the train in question. After stopping dead with the train, the first thing he looked for was a light from the signal box, which was close to. On this particular night he got a signal to set back over the points from the pointsman. He then received a white light from the pointsman and guard, and he set back four or five cGach lengths, before he felt the vacuum brake put on from the van, and he then thought sornetKing was wrong. He and the fireman went down the train, and they found the deceased lying across the rails, four carriages having gone over him. Before setting back he whistled but not loudly.—By Sergeant Longworth : The second signal after stopping at Lowton, he got from the van. He was positive that be got a proper signal from the usual place, and with a proper hand lamp from the van.—By Mr. Bland : He had been in the service of the Company about 26 years, and had been a driver about 19 years. He had been working this train about 12 months. George Hughes Cox, fireman on the engine, corrobo- rated the evidence of the previous witness. He saw a ' white light from the signal box, and also one from the rear of the train out of the van. The engine driver asked him to have a look to see if the signalman ''°Ave a signal to set back, and he got on the tender, and saw a white light in the signal box, and he told the driver to set back. He saw three lamps lying on the ground near deceased, a tail lamp and two hand lamps. The witness Jenkinson was recalled, and in reply to a question said deceased took his hand lamp with him, and he had no other in the van. A verdict of" Accidental death "was returned 'Mk

I presume there is a Surveyor who should visit the district of GrapPenhall and see that the roads are at any rate passable, and there are men kept on the road who are paid for doing the needful. It may be that the Christmas holidays are not quite over yet, or there is a job somewhere else which is of importance to some in- dividual, but not to the community, and they may be attending to that. But during the past three or four weeks the footpaths and highway between "The washer- woman Row" and Leigh Villas has been simply dis- graceful, and would be tolerated in but few places. During the past frcst the greatest caution has been re- quired in passing this spot or a fall was inevitable, the path, and road, being one sheet of ice. Why the farmer should be allowed to permit the water to drain off his field to the inconvenience of all who pass, and to the Injury of the road, is what I fail to comprehend, but hope attention will soon be given to the matter. Another thing that wants looking after is the drains near Turner's farm by Rowson's-lane. Why cannot those drains be cleared, and so prevent the miniature lake which extends over a good part of the road and which is always to be seen after a little rain? Many have had their feet and legs made wet during the present winter by plunging into this pool in the dark, and doubtless have asked with myself—what do we pay our inoney for? Yet another matter. Can any of your numerous readers inform me what heinous crime our ancestors were guilty of, that we, their posterity, should be called upon to do penance in this year of grace 1892? Talk of pilgrimages! Why, it is little less than gross cruelty to allow these round pebbles to remain where they are on the footpath, and to expet men and women to walk on them. Personally, I would get over into the field if I could rather than face the ordeal, and would go any distance around rather than through Grappenhall vil- lage. Such semi-barbaric idias may have suited the past centuries, but they are sadly out of date to-day. In Bellhouse-lane, where the traffic both foot and vehicular is comparatively small, the round stones have been taken up and macadam substituted. It is now a good road. But those bits of fancy pitching are allowed to remain, to the trial of the best of tempers and the punishment of the poor feet. If nothing is done in the matter, I suppose it will be for us as a parish to take the subject before our one, and it seems only chance (for we hear nothing from our County Council representative) the Easter Parochial Council.—l am, Sir, yours, Sze.,
NEMO.

THE PROPOSED DISCUSSION ON EVOLUTION. Sir,—l am obliged to Mr. Peers for his letter of the 2nd inst., but am rather surprised at the tons he has thought proper to adopt. lam afraid he is naturally more satirical than logical. He laughs at my challenge. Probably he finds it easier to laugh than to argue. The modesty upon which he insists so much in others is wanting in his own letter. To identify one's self with scienco and one's opponent with sentiment is certainly a very easy, (though not a very scientific,) mode of pro- cedure. _ .
In answer to his enquiry—l may say I have heard of Icarus ; but does Mr. Peers compare himself with the Sun?

I must disclaim any intention of posing as a champion of orthodogy. By what method has Mr. Peers managed to drag orthodoxy into a discussion of a subject which, in his own words belongs to" the domain of speculation --of philosophic hypothesis 2" "If Mr. Butler wishes to cover himself with glory as the David of orthodoxy by slaying the Goliali of unbelief, let him see to his sling—gather upihis pebbles—slay the unholy giant and wear upon his: modest brow]the laurels of successful polemics." In reply I may say that if I had had any such intention I should most certainly: have selected a more formidable:opponent than Mr. Peers. Mr. Peers declines to discuss the origin of life, and for the following reasons : Firstly, he afraid of being talked to death. Perhaps he feels it as a kind of judgment hanging over him ; such an excuse has a deal of naturalness about it. Secondly He is "not fitted either by having sufficient knowledge or inclination for such a task." This candid admission is good and sufficient reason for declining debate ; but, having made it, Mr. Peers does his utmost to neutralise its force, in the first place by belittling the subject pro- posed for discussion, and secondly, by endeavouring to make his readers believe that I know even less about the subject than he does himself. Now, lam not in the least concerned in defending the immense importance of the doctrine of Abiogenesis—the importance, I mean, to Evolutionists and Philosophers—nor of my own krow- ledge of the doctrine. If anyone were to belittle the atomic theory, or the doctrine of the Conservation of Energy, I should take little notice of him ; and none whatever, if by his own admission he were insufficiently versed in Chemistry and Physics. The doctrine of the Evolution of life is " quite out of the range of practical science " • but the doctrine of the Evolution of man—body soul and spirit—from the Anthromopoid Ape, is of course quite within the range of practical science. Pray what is" practical science "I have not sufficient data upon which to found an argument of any practical value" therefore it is impro- bable that" Mr. W. H. Butler may have, but if so he stands unique among men ; " therefore "Herbert Spencer himself, perhaps the best authority we have on this subject," is'an authority on a subject lacking suffi- cient data, and his arguments are of no" practical value." What is Mr. Peers driving at? Does he knew the case for Evolution ? ot eu of e aTdh to rod nl yo ig oSdu crhe sau dt S buteAllS lOn '‘ would i f buen dae laekr ee nw aws time and type." Mr. Peers has become considerate all of a sudden. There are always plenty of people to be found to decry discussion. I am surprised to find Mr. Peers among their number. "But it is a subject belong- ing to the domain of speculation." Well, what of that? Every subject in its deeper aspects borders on the specu- lative ; and without the discussion in the domain of speculation there could be little or no advance! in science. Controversy is a refining fire. " At present the world is all too young in biological knowledge to furnish materials enough to make this a theme for practical debate." Mr. Peers has fondness for the term" practical" ; thus we have practical science. practical value, and practical debate. However, if he will consult the writings of any of the following, via : Tyndall, Clodd,Maudsley, Grant Allen, Spencer, Huxley, or Weismann, he will find sufficient material to convince him that the world is not so young as he supposes it to be. Mr. Peers then refuses to discuss the doctrine of life from the non-living,and 10 80 doing be will be within his right. He may not believe in the doctrine ;it is impos- sible to say from his letter. On Thursday evening the Rev. W. J. Dawson, of Southport, late of Glasgow, author of "Threshold of Manhood," and editor of "The Young Man," preached at Wycliffe Church, Bewsey-et., Warring- ton, a most impressive and eloquent sermon, from Matthew 24c. and 27 and 28v., "For as the lightning cometh out of the east, and shineth even unto the west, so shall also the coming of the Son of Man be. For whersoever the carcase is there will be the eagles gathered together." There was a good congre- c,ation. The preacher drew an analogy between the agency of ligh.ning and of carrion birds destroying material corruption—and the divine judgments sent upon mankind when in a state of moral corruption. The lightning was sent as the great sanitary officer of nature when the air grew thick and turbid, to destroy the corruption in the atmosphere, so God's ligntnings of judgment were manifested when man became corrupt and the moral purification of the world was necessary. And in the long march of the desert a dead body lay festering, the sky was cloudless, but scarcely had ten minutes passed over the dead body when a little black speck was seen, and presently the vulture descended on its proy,and soon there was nothing left of it but a few white bones bleaching under the fierce sun. So when moral corruption elaued the messengers of divine vengeance were sent like the vulture to punish and destivy. The commonest form of humau error was to think of the judgments of God as though they wc-e ontrolled by no law, or, what was more, in- vent mere theories of law the, result of men's own ignorance. We always found it difficult to distin- guish between judgment and calamity, just as the Jews thought that the men upon whom the tower of Siloam fell were sinners above all men, just as the editor of a certain religious weekly at the time of the Tay Bridge disaster ventured to write an article to prove that it was the visible displeasure of God against the sin of Sunday travelling. When we read such things as these we could not but be thankful that the arrows and fiery bolts of 1 judgment were in wiser hands—in the hands of Him who alone could distinguish where corruption was, and when the hour had come for destruction. The preacher descanted on the erroneous ideas that were held concerning God by which he was made to appear a tyrant and a capricious God, and said the first thing we had to learn about Him was that He worked in a sphere of unalterable and righteous law. There was a wildness in God's mercy like the waves of the sea, but there was also kindness in His justice. He was neitter arbitrary nor caprici- ous in His love or in His judgments. Righteous- ness was sure of divine reward and unrighteous- ness sure of divine retribution. Christ taught that all the forces of the universe were on the side of the good man and against the bad man. It was significent that the words holiness and health sprang from the same root. The holy man was the man who was healthy. Let a man give way to impurity, and the record of his sin was graven upon him in weakness and decay ; and he did not live out his full time. The vultures of retribution were sent from afar. The moral corruption was there, the corrupt framework of the man who was dead in trespasses and sin. Already over some of those present, perchance so high that they could not see him, but still there, the bird of death might be hovering, and unless the process of corruption was stayed by the miracle of God's grace he might drop upon them out of the blue. There was no chance in the calculation. It was the worlotd. an inevitable law, and the vulture was simply the winged judg- ment of God upon pollution. Some few months ago he was permitted to stand in what to him was the most impressive place in modern Europe, the ruins of the buried city of Pompei. You did not need to , read Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire to understand the cause of the great judgment that came upon it; it was written on the walls of ' Pompei in records of altogether unspeakable pol- lution. A quarter of a century ago in the Southern States of America slavery was fast destroying the !national conscience, and the open sore of its exis- tence was poisoning the world. To the unthinking there was no sign of retribution—there was no vis- ible sign of judgment. The blue sky had no thunderclap hanging on it, in the cerulean canopy no one noticed the black spot which was the hover- ing vulture. And yet there were times in the north when the vulture poised in watchful patience above the national sore, In vain the warning was given,in vain the silver trumpet of Longfellow's and Whittier's poetry rang upon the hearts of the nation. They knew that where tt e carcase was there the vulture must be. The hour came when the vulture received the mysterious signal that sent him swoop- ing upon his prey, and under the righ.,eous hand of Gad the pollution of slavery was swept away. Yet more striking was the case of France under the last!empire. Every one knew in those days that Paris had become the moral plague spot of Europe. But few saw the vulture poised in heaven. France had never seemed so strong, her fame was never so brilliant, her power never seemed greater than in the hour when the cry arose in the streets of Paris a Berlin. The judgments of God upon unrighteousness had been wholly forgotten, and no one supposed it possible that within a few months a nation boasting the strongest armaments of Europe should be crushed as it was. It was of importance to recollect how such lessons applied to our own national life. It was so very easy for us to watch the judgments of God upon others. A man might watch a distant thunderstorm with an aesthetic sense of its grandeur, forgetting that the lightning travelled from east to west and was no respecter of persons. He sometimes thought there were ele- ments in our national life to-day that were making us ready for the judgment that came upon corrupt , peoples. Think of the mad race for wealth, the ' iniquities of our commerce, the profligacy, the drunkenness,the!heartlessness to the cry of suffering, our selfishness, and see if there were no signs of retribution, no indication in the heavens that the vulture was already poised. He prayed heaven it might not be so. The rev, gentleman in conclud- ing addressed a few words to the young men of his congregation, urging on them that if they would be the saviours of the future, they must ground themselves on the principl, that God lived and was righteous, and that the only greatness for indivi- duals or nations was in righteousness. This was the soul of the old Puritanism, and it must be the animating spirit of the new.—The Rev. J. Yonge took pert in the service, and closed it with the Benediction.

rRIMITIVE MUTHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL .—The annual the party in connection with the Primitive Methodist Sunday School was held on Monday evening,when a good number sat down to tea. After tea, an entertaiment was given by the choir and scholars, consisting of recit- ations, dialogues, anthems, and a laughing chorus, the last-named being encored. The chair was taken by Mr. G. L. Welford, who said that there was an increase of six in the membership, after striking off the names of - the old scholars.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST AN ASSIS-
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST AN ASSIS-
TANT BANK CASHIER.

George Aaron Fairhurst, residing at Grappenhall, was charged on Monday, at Manchester, with steal- ing nearly £2OO from the Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank, Spring Gardens. The prisoner was an assis- tant cashier at the bank, and as such he was en- trusted with £2OO worth of silver, to be used for changing purposes, and which he kept in a private safe. The money was kept in three bags, one con- taining one hundred pounds and the other two fifty pounds each. On the 14th of last month Fairhurst was required temporarily to take the place of an official at the Warrington branch where he was formerly stationed, and in his absence his safe and three bags of silver was handed over to another. cashier. Before leaving the prisoner requested that gentleman not to deal with the money until his re- turn from Warrington. The request was complied with for the time being, but subsequently the pri- soner's deputy became uneasy, and on Saturday the three bags in the safe were opened, and instead of silver were found to contain copper of the value of £8 15s.—Mr. Charles Lumsdale, sub-manager at the bank, saw the prisoner the same evening, and he then admitted having taken the money.—Mr. R. Gobbett, who defended, said the prisoner had been in the service of the bank for twelve or thirteen years, and had lately been in receipt of a salary of £l4O a year. Although the prisoner had taken the money, he had not taken it in gambling or any- thing of that kind, but seemed to have lived beyond his means. He found himself in. difficulties, and had taken the money to meet household expenses. -Up to the commission of that offence the prisoncr had been perfectly steady and respectable. He (Mr. Cobbett) also understood the bank authorities did not wish that a severe sentence should be passed.— The Stipendiary Magistrate thought justice in the case would be met by a sentence of one month's imprisonment. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.

The first of the international contests plainly demon- strated the superiority of the English fifteeen over their Welsh rivals. Seventeen points to none is decisive enongh in all conscience. The game proved very attra- tive to the Londoners, and there was a big crowd at Blackheath enclosure. The beautiful afternoon had doubtless something to do with the attendance, and the football was carried on amid surroundings that are not often met with at this time of the year.

In congratulating ourselves on the result we must not overtook the absence of the brothers James from the Welsh team. The two Swansea half backs are such very smart players that their presence must have made a diff- erence. Taylor's loss from the other side was not so serious, as it brought the two Bradford halves together, which was in some respects an advantage. Still,neither Briggs nor Emmott struck one as being above the com- mon order, and the first-named was often guilty of off- side tactics,as he was in the fixture between Lancashire and Yorkshire. The English backs were if anything better than the forward division, the latter being some- times nonplussed by the Welsh method of !wheeling the scrimmages. Indeed forward Wales compared very favourably with their antagonists. Bancroft was on the whole a safer full back than Thompson, and Pearson and Gold were very smart at threequarters. The tack- ling of the English backs left little to be desired, and some of Hubbard's runs delighted the southerners. Lockwood did his work well, and occasionally Alderson was very effective.

Cheshire can hardly flatter themselves that they pulled off their match with Cumberland by superior football. The better county did not win in this case. The for- wards of the northern shire gave, a splendid account of themselves, and Murchie, the Workington half-back, played magnificently. ,Cheshire excelled in combination behind the scrimmage. The score reads curiously—two goals (one dropped) and one try to one goal (dropped) and two tries.

Swinton put the four three-quarters system, into operation against the Barbarians, St. Helens Recreation, and Moseley. They won all the matches easily. Marsh was not available, as he had been bedfast with a severe cold. In the game with the " Recs." both sides were very weak, and Swinton spored heavily, Valentine and Simpson being each credited with a couple of tries. Valentine secured three tries against the Barbarians and the feature in this game being another against Moseley, the faulty place kicking, three chances being all missed. Swinton are just now in very fine form. 1 Broughton has also been guilty of feeble place kicking. It was to this that they had to ascribe their defeat by Blackley Rangers. In their fixture with Birkenhead Park their efforts were pitiable. Not a single goal' out of five tries was a poor afternoon's work. A reliable goal kicker is badly wanted. Broughton Rangers were not very seriously tested by endleton, the verdict being in their favovr by twelve points to four. A dropped goal alone represented the extent of the victory of Broughton Park over the Free Wanderers. Oldham can hardly have bargained fcr defeat by Millom.

The strugele for the League championship had practi- cally settled ifself into a duel between the North End and Sunderland. The North End was triumphant at both Darwen and Sccringt.on. They not only improved their position by an addition of four points but materially raised their goal average. The first champions of the League have not lost a game since the last Saturday in September, during which time they have registered no fewer than 25 points. Sunderland were not playing on Saturday—indeed they will be idle until January 23,and the Boltonians have not another league fixture until the first of March.

After staying in Manchester on Friday night Derby County journeyed to Blackburn, when they surprised everybody by beating the Rovers. The football was of a poor quality all round, the home forwards doing very badly. They missed openings in a disgraceful fashion. Johnny Goodall was again an absentee, and the Rovers were without Forbes and Forest. The two clubs are to meet again in the F.A. cup competition. January 16.

Seeing that Everton could visit Aston Villa in the early part of the week and win their Loague fixture their friends naturally expected them to polish off Burnley at Anfield on Saturday. But they didn't. They had to rest satisfied with a draw, having gone through a like experience with Kilmarnock on New Year's Day. Aston Villa were easily vanquished by Notts County on SAtur- day, the victors playing in better style than at any time this season. The popularity of football in the:lace town is shown by the fact that the contest between Notts and Notts Forest on Boxing Day realised £5O.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
The monthly meeting of this Committee was held yesterday at the workhouse, Mr. Balharry presid- ing. Several appeals were'dealt with, but nothing of public interest arose in connection with them.

div.p: THE PEARL CASE.
_ The " Dublin Express " says Captain Osborne retires on half-pay, and goes abroad immediately. RUNCORN SCHOONETI. ABANDONED. _
The Schooner Saint of Runcorn was seen disrnasted off Lynmouth yesterday morning. The crew were rescued by the lifeboat.
RANDOLPH HOME AGAIN,

Yesterday Lord Randolph Churchill arrived at Southampton from South Africa, and was met by Lady Randolph Churchill. COLLISION OFF THE TYNE. The large Newcastle steamer Crystal was sunk in col- lision with the steamer off the Tyne on Thursday night. The crew were saved.
THE DUKE OF_CLARENCE'S BIRTHDAY.,
The 28th birthday of the Duke of Clarence was cele- brated at Windsor, yesterday, by the ringing of bells and the firing of a royal salute. THE SNOW STORM.

Continued snowfallis reported from various parts of the country. In and about Bolton travelling is difficult, and, there, as also at Holyhead and elsewhere, traffic has been considerably affected. THE ROSSENDALE ELECTION., The result of a conference yesterday between political agents on both sides was to ask the Sheriff to fix the 23rd inst. as the day of polling; and, if adopted, counting and declaration will be announced the same day.

DISTINGUISHED PATIENTS. The Bishop of St. Asaph continues to improve. Lord Deramore's condition has slightly improved. Dr. Philpott, late Bishop of Worcester,who is suffering from chronic illness incidental to his great age; was rather weaker yesterday. THE WHALLEY FRAUDS. Mr. S. Mather, the solicitor who was authorised by Vice-Chancellor Bristowe to receive claims against the estate of the late Mr. H. S. Whalley, solicitor, of Black- burn, has had deposited with him no fewer than 322' claims, which are being carefully investigated. Many of them are for large sums, but it will take sometime to ascertain the total amount of the liabilities.

MR. HASTINGS, M.P., AT BOW-STREET. At Bow-street Police Court, yesterday, Mr. Hastings,. M.P. fer East Worcestershire, was again charged with defrauding the beneficiaries under the will of the late Major John Brown of 215,000.—Mr5. Charlotte A. Graze- brock, widow of the Jbeneficiaries, stated that defendant had paid her dividends up to July, 1890. She first heard of the re-investment of £15,000 in the Palsall Company in spring last.—Detective-Inspector Moore then proved the arrest of the prisoner, who was further remanded for the attendance of another witness.—The magistrate- agreed to accept bail, two sureties of £5,000 and the prisoner in £lO,OOO.

COLLIERY DISASTER. REPORTED ENTOMBMENT OF 200 MINERS. NIW Yon, FRIDAY.—A serious explosion occurred yesterday, in a mine near Krebs, in Indian territory. It is reported that 200 miners are entombed. A later telegram says ten dead bodies have been ex, tricated.

div.head: AGED FOLK'S CHRSITMAS TREATS.
div.p: AGED FOLK'S CHRSITMAS TREATS.

The annual Christmas treats to the aged folk of Warrington were held in the Public Hall, on Thurs- day. About 450 old men were entertained to ar. sumptuous dinner, with beer if they preferred it, they being allowed as an alternative an extra quan- tity of tobacco after dinner. -All the members of the committee were present, together with their wives, and included the following :—Alderman Sut- ton (president), Mr. Thomas Jones (vice-president), Mr. Thomas Morris (hon. treasurer), Alderman Wright (hon. secretary), Messrs. P. Caldwell, P. Chrimes, S. Jones, D. Jones, D. Fanshawe, and C. Skinner, Councillor J. Smethurst, and Messrs. G. Pilling and W. H. Robinson. There were also pre- sent the Rev, F. W. Willis, rector of Warrington ; the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, the Rev. W. E. Glen,vicar of St. Mary's, Bank Quay; the Rev, IL V. Pigot, vicar of St. Paul's; the Rev. Father Feeney, Alder- man and Mrs. Harrison, Councillor Plumpton, and Dr. Cannell, Councillor and Miss Ashton, Mrs. R. Chapman, Mr. G. Parr, Mrs. Clare, Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Woods, Mr. H. Toft, Mr. and Mrs. Gill, Mr. and Mrs. Litton, Messrs. Rankin, and S. B. Stringer. and Mr. G. Riley. Aldermati SUTTON, on behalf of the Committee expressed the pleasure they felt at seeing the old men present, and wished them a happy New Year. He proposed the toast of " the Queen, which toast was drunk with hearty cheers.—The Rev. F. W. Wrz.xis then addressed a few remarks to the aged men.—Sergeant HARDY, one of the aged men, and an old Crimean soldier, in an excellent speech thanked the Committee on behalf of the old men.— Mr. THOS. MORRIS moved a cordial vote Of thanks to the subscribers, and this was heartily given.—A sb.rig "Tom Bowling," was then sung in very good style by Mr. G. Parr, after which the company dis- persed. At six o'clock in the evening the aged women were entertained to tea in the Public Hall, the number present being considerably in excess of the previous year. The hall was crowded. All the members of the committee,with their wives, were in attendance, and among those present were also the -I.'ev. F. Slater, of St. James's, the Rev. M.. Stapylton, his curate, Councillor Ashton and Mrs. Joseph Harrison. In the evening the usual meeting and entertainment were held.—Alderman Sutton on behalf of the committee welcomed the old women and wished them a very happy and prosperous new year. (Applause) Every year they seemed to have more applications for tickets, and hundreds had to be turned away that night. That year they were more numerous than ever before, and something more would have to be done if they were to provide for the annually increasing applications they had. Alderman Sutton created much amuse- ment by describing the difficulty the committee had in ascertaining the ages of some of the applicants. One old lady said she was 73, and they gave her a ;icket, and she said "Please could'nt you give me

_ one for my mother?" (Great laughter.) Thy could not say whether the old lady really was 72i but they got to know who her mother was and she was somewhere about 90. Somebody ma;le the ob- servation to her daughter, " Well, you have got one for yourself and one for your mother; what about your grandmother ? " " Oh," she said," my grandmother is deact ;she died two or three weeks ago." (Roars of laughter.) Alderman Sutton pointed out that the receipts of the Committee, last year were £93 3s. ld.,and the expenditure wa5...296 6s. Id.' leaving an excess-over income of .E 3 3s. He thought that when they were able to feast over li,ooo people and mere only ..C,3,35. out of pocket,amigave .£25 be- sides for the benefit of the poor as they did they had done very well.—On the motiostiof Mr. Thomas Morris, seconded by Alderman Sutton, a vote of thanks to the subscribers was carried with acclama- tion. A concert was subsequently given which was succeeded by an amusing farce entitled" The area belle." We may mention that Mr. G. Riley, and Mr-. W. S. Woods, organist,contributed their musical ser- vices in connection with the treats.

PROMOTION TOTS THE S. nELENS, STATIONMASTER:. Mr. David Moss, stationmaster, St. Helens, has been appoktted stationmaster at Edgehill, in successicin to the rate Mr. James Stewart. Mr. Moss is a, native of Uttoxeter, Staffordshire, wad has been in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company 36 years. He commenced as porter at Euston, aril held a yosition as guard for 15 years travelling over all parts of. the system. He then took extraordinary duties as , relief snationmaster, and was in. the superi sten dent's office at Lime.st.,whan 16 yee,es since, he was appointed stationmaster at St, Helens. Mr. Moss was electd out of a great number of applicants for the Edgehill vacancy. During his residence in St. Helens Mr. Moss has made hosts of friends by his geniality and courtesy, combined with strong sense of duty,and perhapsthere is no official 1 in the district better known or more highly esteemed. He will leave St. Helens for Edgehill with the best wishes of manufacturers, tradesmen, and the general public. inspector Bolton, of Oarston is mentioned as the probable successor 0 Mr., Moss at St. ilelams..

WHY DOES A WOMAN LOOK OLD , BEFORE HER HUSBAND? Every woman who has her• own housework to do knows that washing-day is the chief cause of the careworn look, broken health, and premature old age, noticeable in so many of her sex. Many a woman has to bend over a steaming wash-tub full of soiled clothes—to boil all the forenoon, and rub all the afternoon—and while still warm and perspiring from the hot, filthy steam, run out into the cold—bare- headed and bare-armed—to hang up the clothes on a freezing line. This is done, not once, but week after week, and the wonder is how any woman lives through it—many don't! The sudden change from the hot, perspiring labour and wet steaming room inside to the cold air outside produces the natural result: a cold, followed quickly by pneumonia or diphtheria, or some kindred disease, ending in the death of the poor victim. Friends call it a dispensation of Providence. What the woman actually died of was poor soap, hard labour, and exposure.
